questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clause 5.2 (Policy); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.1 (Policies for Information Security); COBIT 2019 APO01 (Managed I&T Management Framework)
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a newly issued information security policy. Which finding should concern the auditor MOST?

options.A: The policy does not name the firewall products in use
options.B: The policy was issued without approval from senior management
options.C: The policy does not state how often it will be reviewed
options.D: The policy leaves server configuration steps to separate standards

questions.key_concept: An information security policy gets its authority from senior management approval; it stays high level and leaves technical detail to standards.
questions.pre_read: Ask which finding means the policy has no force at all, and which ones are fixable gaps or good practice.
questions.correct_explanation: A policy draws its authority from management. Without senior management approval, staff and system owners have no mandate to follow it, and every standard beneath it lacks backing. ISO/IEC 27001 makes top management responsible for establishing the policy. A missing review interval is a real gap that lets the policy go stale, but it can be fixed at the next revision, while an unapproved policy has no force today.

wrong_explanations.A: Naming products would itself be a mistake. A policy should be technology-neutral so it survives tool changes; product detail belongs in standards.
wrong_explanations.C: A defined review cycle matters and its absence should be fixed, but the policy still carries authority while its content remains current.
wrong_explanations.D: This is the correct document hierarchy. Policies state intent, and lower-level standards and procedures hold the configuration detail.

tips: Eliminate: A describes detail a policy should leave out, and D describes the proper split between policy and standards.
Final two: B beats C because a policy without management approval has no authority, while a missing review cycle only risks it going stale later.
Exam cue: for policy questions, management endorsement comes first; content and upkeep matter once the policy carries authority.

questions.subtopic: Information Security Frameworks. ISO 27001 vs NIST CSF
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (Information Security Management Systems); NIST Cybersecurity Framework (NIST CSF) v2.0 (February 2024)
questions.question: A CIO must give major customers independent, certifiable assurance that the organization runs a sound information security management system. Which approach BEST meets this need?

options.A: Align the security program with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework
options.B: Commission an external penetration test of internet-facing systems
options.C: Assess IT service processes against an ITIL maturity model
options.D: Certify the management system against ISO/IEC 27001 requirements

questions.key_concept: ISO/IEC 27001 is a certifiable management-system standard; the NIST Cybersecurity Framework is a voluntary, outcome-based framework without certification.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word certifiable in the stem. Ask which option produces a certificate that an independent body can issue.
questions.correct_explanation: ISO/IEC 27001 sets requirements for an information security management system, and an accredited certification body can certify conformance, giving customers independent assurance. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is a strong, widely used way to organize cyber risk outcomes, but it is voluntary and has no certification scheme, so alignment with it remains a self-declared claim. The customer need for certifiable assurance decides between them.

wrong_explanations.A: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is voluntary and risk-focused. It offers no formal certification, so alignment cannot give customers certifiable assurance.
wrong_explanations.B: A penetration test gives a point-in-time technical view of some systems. It says nothing about whether the whole management system works.
wrong_explanations.C: ITIL addresses IT service management, not information security management, and a maturity assessment is not a certification.

tips: Eliminate: B is a narrow technical test, and C covers service management rather than security management.
Final two: D beats A because only ISO/IEC 27001 offers accredited certification of the whole management system, while framework alignment stays self-declared.
Exam cue: when the stem asks for certifiable or third-party assurance, look for a standard with an accredited certification scheme.

questions.framework_ref: ISACA CISA Review Manual, 28th Edition, Chapter 5 (Protection of Information Assets); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-14 (Environmental Controls); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.5 (Protecting Against Physical and Environmental Threats)
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews environmental controls in a company data center. Which finding represents the GREATEST risk?

options.A: Temperature and humidity alarms are not monitored by anyone
options.B: The fire suppression inspection is two months overdue
options.C: Visitors sign the entry log but not the exit log
options.D: Backup tapes are encrypted with an outdated algorithm

questions.key_concept: Environmental controls cover heat, humidity, water, fire and power, and each needs monitoring that alerts someone able to respond.
questions.pre_read: First sort the options into environmental and non-environmental. Then ask which environmental gap could cause damage nobody notices.
questions.correct_explanation: Environmental controls only protect equipment if someone learns of a problem in time. Alarms that nobody monitors mean an overheating or humidity fault can run unnoticed until hardware fails. An overdue fire suppression inspection is a real gap that needs scheduling, but the system is still installed and likely to work, so the exposure is smaller than conditions that nobody sees.

wrong_explanations.B: A short inspection delay is a compliance gap to schedule promptly. The system remains in place and is likely still functional.
wrong_explanations.C: An incomplete visitor log is a physical access weakness, not an environmental control issue such as heat, water, fire or power.
wrong_explanations.D: Weak backup encryption is a logical security issue. It does not affect environmental protection of the data center.

tips: Eliminate: C is a physical access issue and D is a cryptography issue; neither is an environmental control.
Final two: A beats B because unmonitored alarms let damage happen unseen, while a slightly late inspection leaves a working system in place.
Exam cue: an environmental control that nobody watches gives no protection; detection must reach someone who can act.

questions.framework_ref: ISACA CISA Review Manual, 28th Edition, Chapter 5 (Protection of Information Assets); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-3 (Physical Access Control); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.2 (Physical Entry)
questions.question: A security manager must restrict entry to a network wiring closet so that each entry is traceable to a person and access can be withdrawn quickly. Which control BEST meets this need?

options.A: Warning signs saying the closet is under constant surveillance
options.B: A camera recording everyone who opens the closet door
options.C: A badge-controlled lock limited to named network staff
options.D: A keyed lock with keys held by the network team

questions.key_concept: Physical controls are deterrent, preventive or detective; the best preventive control also supports individual accountability and fast revocation.
questions.pre_read: Classify each option as deterrent, preventive or detective. Then weigh the two preventive options against traceability and quick withdrawal.
questions.correct_explanation: Both locks prevent entry, but only a badge-controlled lock ties each opening to a named person and lets access be removed at once by disabling a badge. Physical keys can be copied or lent, leave no record of who used them, and must be recovered, or the lock changed, when someone leaves. The stem's need for traceability and quick withdrawal decides it.

wrong_explanations.A: Signs are a deterrent control. They discourage entry but cannot stop or record anyone who ignores them.
wrong_explanations.B: A camera is a detective control. It records who entered after the fact but does not restrict entry to the closet.
wrong_explanations.D: A keyed lock is preventive, but keys can be copied or shared, their use is not logged, and withdrawing access means recovering keys or rekeying.

tips: Eliminate: A only deters and B only detects; neither restricts entry.
Final two: C beats D because badge access is logged to individuals and can be revoked at once, while keys cannot.
Exam cue: sort physical controls by type first (deter, prevent, detect), then choose the preventive control that also gives accountability.

questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clause 5.2 (Policy); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.1 (Policies for Information Security)
questions.question: A CISO reviews the information security policy every November, and a new data protection law affecting it takes effect in March. What should the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Ask staff to re-acknowledge the current policy text
options.B: Start an out-of-cycle review of the policy for the law
options.C: Log the new law for the scheduled November policy review
options.D: Have the legal team amend the policy without management sign-off

questions.key_concept: Policies are reviewed on a set cycle and also whenever a significant change, such as a new law, makes them outdated.
questions.pre_read: Compare the law's start date with the next scheduled review. Ask how long the policy would be out of date if you waited.
questions.correct_explanation: Policy review has two triggers: a fixed cycle and significant change. A law that takes effect in March would leave the policy out of line for about eight months if the CISO waited for November, so a change-triggered review is needed now. Logging the law for the annual review is orderly, but it lets the organization run on an outdated policy while the law already applies.

wrong_explanations.A: Re-acknowledging the old text spreads awareness of a policy that will soon be out of line with the law. It changes nothing.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for the annual cycle leaves the policy misaligned with the law for months after it takes effect.
wrong_explanations.D: Policy changes need management approval to carry authority. Legal input is valuable, but it cannot replace management sign-off.

tips: Eliminate: A only re-circulates an outdated policy, and D skips the management approval every policy revision needs.
Final two: B beats C because a significant legal change triggers review now, while the annual cycle would leave a months-long gap.
Exam cue: periodic review is a minimum; a major change in law, business or threat triggers an earlier review.

questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.31 (Legal, Statutory, Regulatory and Contractual Requirements); COBIT 2019 MEA03 (Managed Compliance with External Requirements); NIST Cybersecurity Framework (NIST CSF) v2.0 (February 2024)
questions.question: A newly appointed CISO at an EU payment processor must choose an information security framework. What should the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Identify the legal and contractual security requirements that apply
options.B: Compare the control coverage of the leading security frameworks
options.C: Adopt the framework the CISO used at a previous employer
options.D: Ask the external auditor to select the most defensible framework

questions.key_concept: Choose a security framework by first identifying binding legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, then evaluating which framework meets them.
questions.pre_read: Look for the step that every other step depends on. Ask what you would compare the frameworks against.
questions.correct_explanation: Framework choice should start from what the organization must meet. An EU payment processor is likely to face data protection law and card industry obligations, and these set the minimum any framework must cover. Comparing control coverage is a sound step, but without the requirements first there is nothing to measure coverage against, so the comparison may favor a framework that misses a mandatory obligation.

wrong_explanations.B: Comparing coverage is useful, but done first it has no yardstick. Requirements must be known before frameworks can be judged against them.
wrong_explanations.C: A familiar framework may not fit this organization's laws, contracts or risks. Personal preference is not a selection criterion.
wrong_explanations.D: Selecting the framework is a management decision. An external auditor who chose it would later be auditing their own choice, impairing independence.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on personal habit, and D hands a management decision to the auditor.
Final two: A beats B because requirements are the yardstick; comparing frameworks before knowing them puts the analysis before the need.
Exam cue: for selection questions, start with the requirements (legal, regulatory, contractual), then evaluate options against them.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-6 (Configuration Settings); CIS Controls v8 Control 4 (Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets); COBIT 2019 BAI10 (Managed Configuration)
questions.question: A security manager uses CIS Benchmarks as configuration baselines, but a legacy payroll server cannot support one required setting without breaking its application. What is the BEST approach?

options.A: Remove the setting from the baseline for every server
options.B: Leave the server noncompliant until its next hardware refresh
options.C: Move the server onto an isolated network segment
options.D: Approve a documented exception with a compensating control

questions.key_concept: Configuration baselines need a formal exception process: documented, risk-accepted by the owner, and backed by compensating controls.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option keeps the deviation visible and accepted by someone accountable, rather than only reducing it technically.
questions.correct_explanation: Baselines need a managed exception path. Documenting the exception, having the risk owner accept it, and adding a compensating control keeps the deviation visible, approved and reviewed. Isolating the server may well be the right compensating control, but done alone it is an undocumented technical fix: nobody formally accepts the residual risk, and the deviation disappears from the baseline record.

wrong_explanations.A: Dropping the setting for every server weakens the whole estate to accommodate one legacy system.
wrong_explanations.B: Waiting for a refresh leaves an unrecorded, unaccepted gap for an unknown period.
wrong_explanations.C: Isolation may reduce the risk, but without a documented, approved exception nobody accepts the residual risk and the gap is untracked.

tips: Eliminate: A weakens every server for one exception, and B leaves an unmanaged gap with no end date.
Final two: D beats C because a governed exception records and accepts the risk, while isolation alone is an untracked technical workaround.
Exam cue: when a system cannot meet a standard, look for a documented, approved exception with compensating controls.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.3 (Segregation of Duties)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that one accounts payable clerk can create new vendors and approve payments to them. Which recommendation BEST addresses this risk?

options.A: Require multi-factor authentication for the clerk's system login
options.B: Review a monthly report of payments to newly created vendors
options.C: Assign vendor creation and payment approval to different staff
options.D: Encrypt the vendor master file stored in the database

questions.key_concept: Segregation of duties prevents one person from completing a sensitive process alone; detective reviews are a fallback, not a substitute.
questions.pre_read: Name the two duties in the stem. Ask which option stops one person holding both, rather than spotting misuse later.
questions.correct_explanation: Creating a vendor and approving payments to it are incompatible duties: together they let one person set up a fictitious supplier and pay it. Separating the duties prevents that fraud path at the source. A monthly report of payments to new vendors is a useful detective control, but it finds problems only after money has left and relies on someone acting on the report.

wrong_explanations.A: Stronger authentication confirms who the clerk is. It does not limit what the clerk is authorized to do.
wrong_explanations.B: A monthly review is detective. It finds fictitious vendors after payment, while the conflicting access remains in place.
wrong_explanations.D: Encryption protects data confidentiality. It does nothing about one person holding both incompatible duties.

tips: Eliminate: A strengthens authentication and D protects confidentiality; neither removes the conflicting duties.
Final two: C beats B because separating the duties prevents the fraud, while a monthly report only detects it afterwards.
Exam cue: when one person holds incompatible duties, prefer removing the conflict over adding a later review.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev 1 (Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments); ISO/IEC 27005:2022 (Information Security Risk Management); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.5 (Protecting Against Physical and Environmental Threats)
questions.question: A data center manager is starting an environmental exposure assessment covering fire, water, power and cooling. What should the manager do FIRST?

options.A: Identify critical equipment and the hazards facing each area
options.B: Buy additional leak and smoke sensors for every room
options.C: Test the existing controls against last year's incident log
options.D: Adopt the hazard list from a peer firm's assessment

questions.key_concept: An environmental exposure assessment follows risk-assessment order: assets and hazards first, then existing controls, then residual risk and remediation.
questions.pre_read: Put the options in the order a risk assessment runs. Then ask which one must come before the others.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk assessment starts by knowing what must be protected and from what. Listing critical equipment and the fire, water, power and cooling hazards in each area tells the manager which controls matter most. Testing existing controls is a necessary later step, but without the asset and hazard picture there is no basis for judging whether those controls cover the right risks.

wrong_explanations.B: Buying sensors before assessing risk puts technology ahead of analysis and may spend money where the exposure is low.
wrong_explanations.C: Control testing comes after assets and hazards are known; otherwise the test may confirm controls that do not address the real exposures.
wrong_explanations.D: Another firm's hazards differ in layout, location and equipment, so a borrowed list can miss this site's actual exposures.

tips: Eliminate: B buys technology before assessing risk, and D borrows a hazard list that does not fit this site.
Final two: A beats C because assets and hazards must be known before controls can be judged against them.
Exam cue: in any risk assessment, identify assets and threats first, then evaluate controls, then prioritize the gaps.

questions.framework_ref: NFPA 75 (Standard for the Fire Protection of Information Technology Equipment); NFPA 2001 (Standard on Clean Agent Fire Extinguishing Systems)
questions.question: A data center manager must choose fire suppression for a server room where staff regularly work. Which option BEST protects people and avoids damaging the servers if it discharges?

options.A: Wet-pipe sprinklers with water held permanently in the pipes
options.B: A clean-agent gas system with very early smoke detection
options.C: Pre-action sprinklers whose dry pipes fill after two separate alarms
options.D: A carbon dioxide flooding system covering the whole room

questions.key_concept: For occupied server rooms, clean-agent gas suppression protects people and equipment; pre-action sprinklers are the preferred water-based option.
questions.pre_read: Underline the two constraints in the stem: people present and equipment damage. Test each option against both.
questions.correct_explanation: A clean-agent gas system puts out fire without water and is designed to be safe for people at its design concentration, so it protects both staff and servers, and very early smoke detection lets staff respond before discharge. Pre-action sprinklers are the safer water option because their pipes stay dry until two alarms confirm a fire, but once they discharge, water still damages the equipment.

wrong_explanations.A: Wet pipes discharge water directly onto equipment and can leak or trigger accidentally, causing the damage the stem wants to limit.
wrong_explanations.C: Pre-action reduces accidental discharge, but when it does release, water still damages the servers.
wrong_explanations.D: Carbon dioxide flooding displaces oxygen and can kill people, so it is unsuitable for a room where staff regularly work.

tips: Eliminate: A sprays water on equipment, and D endangers anyone in the room.
Final two: B beats C because a clean agent leaves equipment undamaged, while pre-action only delays water until discharge.
Exam cue: read the constraint words; people present rules out carbon dioxide, and limiting equipment damage favors a clean agent over water.

questions.framework_ref: NFPA 110 (Standard for Emergency and Standby Power Systems); Uptime Institute Tier Standard: Topology; NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-11 (Emergency Power)
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews power protection for a data center that must keep running through utility outages lasting several days. Which design weakness is MOST significant?

options.A: Power distribution unit loads are reviewed monthly, not weekly
options.B: Backup batteries are replaced on the manufacturer's schedule
options.C: The generator has no battery system to bridge its start-up
options.D: The battery system has no generator to carry long outages

questions.key_concept: Batteries bridge short gaps and generator start-up; only generators with fuel sustain power through long outages, so both are needed.
questions.pre_read: Note the outage length in the stem. Ask which weakness makes it impossible to stay up for days.
questions.correct_explanation: Batteries carry the load for minutes, not days. Without a generator, a multi-day utility outage ends in a full shutdown once the batteries drain, so the data center cannot meet its stated need. A generator with no battery bridge is also a real gap: systems may drop for the seconds it takes to start. That interruption is brief and recoverable, while the missing generator makes loss of power certain.

wrong_explanations.A: Monthly load reviews are a minor monitoring choice. They do not stop power reaching the equipment during an outage.
wrong_explanations.B: Following the manufacturer's replacement schedule is good practice. It keeps batteries able to carry the load when needed.
wrong_explanations.C: A missing bridge causes a brief drop while the generator starts. That is serious but recoverable, unlike running out of power entirely.

tips: Eliminate: A is a minor monitoring choice, and B describes good maintenance practice.
Final two: D beats C because batteries last minutes, so without a generator a multi-day outage means certain shutdown; a missing bridge causes only a brief drop.
Exam cue: match the control to the duration in the stem; batteries bridge seconds to minutes, generators carry hours to days.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-2 (Physical Access Authorizations); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.2 (Physical Entry); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)
questions.question: An IS auditor has limited time to test whether data center access is restricted to authorized staff. Which procedure provides the BEST evidence?

options.A: Review the badge system's uptime and vendor reports
options.B: Observe staff badging in at the entrance for one morning
options.C: Compare the badge access list with current staff and roles
options.D: Inspect the fire marshal's certificate for the building

questions.key_concept: Strong access evidence comes from comparing the full list of access rights with an authoritative source such as current HR records.
questions.pre_read: Ask which procedure would catch a former employee whose badge still works but who did not come in that day.
questions.correct_explanation: Comparing the full badge access list with current staff records and roles tests everyone who can get in, revealing leavers, transfers and unexplained grants. Observation shows how people behave on one morning: it cannot reveal a former employee whose badge still works, or a contractor with access who simply did not visit that day, so it gives weaker evidence.

wrong_explanations.A: Uptime figures and vendor reports show the system is available. They give no evidence about who is allowed in.
wrong_explanations.B: Observation covers a single period and the people who happened to enter. Unauthorized badges that went unused stay hidden.
wrong_explanations.D: A fire certificate relates to life safety and building compliance, not to whether access is limited to authorized staff.

tips: Eliminate: A measures availability and D concerns fire safety; neither tests who can enter.
Final two: C beats B because comparing the whole access list with staff records tests every authorized badge, while observation sees one morning.
Exam cue: for who-has-access objectives, testing the access list against an authoritative source beats watching activity.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-8 (Visitor Access Records); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-3 (Physical Access Control); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.2 (Physical Entry)
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews visitor controls at a data center that hosts customer payment systems. Which finding should concern the auditor MOST?

options.A: Walk-in visitors are admitted without approval from any employee
options.B: Visitor departure times are often missing from the paper sign-in log
options.C: Visitors wait in reception until their host collects them
options.D: Visitor badges are a different color from employee badges

questions.key_concept: Visitor management rests on prior authorization by a named host, supported by identification, escort, distinct badges and complete logs.
questions.pre_read: Separate good practices from weaknesses. Then rank the weaknesses: a missing gate versus an incomplete record.
questions.correct_explanation: Visitor control starts with authorization: a named employee should approve each visit in advance and take responsibility for the visitor. Admitting walk-ins with no approval lets anyone reach a site holding payment systems. Missing departure times weaken the record and make investigations harder, but those visitors were still approved and hosted, so the risk is smaller than letting unapproved strangers in.

wrong_explanations.B: An incomplete log is a detective weakness that hampers investigation. The visitors were still authorized on arrival.
wrong_explanations.C: Holding visitors in reception until the host arrives is good practice that keeps them out of secure areas.
wrong_explanations.D: Distinct badge colors are good practice, letting staff spot visitors and challenge them in restricted areas.

tips: Eliminate: C and D describe sound visitor practices, not weaknesses.
Final two: A beats B because missing authorization lets unknown people in, while missing exit times only weaken the record.
Exam cue: in visitor management, prior authorization by a named host is the foundation; logs and badges support it.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-3 (Physical Access Control); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.2 (Physical Entry)
questions.question: A CISO learns that staff routinely hold the server room door open for colleagues who have not badged in. Which control BEST prevents this tailgating?

options.A: A stricter approval process before issuing new staff badges
options.B: Cameras over the door with recordings kept for ninety days
options.C: Annual awareness training telling staff not to hold the door
options.D: A mantrap that admits one badged person at a time

questions.key_concept: Tailgating is best prevented by physical controls such as mantraps that enforce one person per authentication, supported by awareness training.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem describes a routine habit. Ask which option still works when staff keep being polite.
questions.correct_explanation: Tailgating here is a habit of courtesy, so the strongest fix removes the opportunity rather than asking people to change. A mantrap physically admits one authenticated person at a time, whatever staff intend. Awareness training is a sensible support, but it depends on busy people remembering to refuse colleagues, and a yearly session fades quickly.

wrong_explanations.A: Badge issuance controls who gets a badge. It does nothing about staff letting unbadged people follow them through.
wrong_explanations.B: Cameras record tailgating after it happens. They do not stop anyone from following staff inside.
wrong_explanations.C: Training helps but relies on staff behavior, the very weakness in the stem; it cannot physically stop a follower.

tips: Eliminate: A tightens badge issuance and B only records events; neither stops someone following staff through.
Final two: D beats C because a mantrap enforces one-at-a-time entry, while training depends on the habits that are already failing.
Exam cue: when the problem is routine human behavior, prefer an engineered control that removes the opportunity over asking people to try harder.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-6 (Monitoring Physical Access); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.4 (Physical Security Monitoring)
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the closed-circuit television program for a data center. Which finding should concern the auditor MOST?

options.A: Staff watch the camera feeds live during nights and weekends
options.B: Guards on duty can delete recorded footage without approval
options.C: Camera clocks drift several minutes from the badge system
options.D: Recordings are kept for sixty days before being overwritten

questions.key_concept: Camera recordings must be protected from alteration or deletion, especially by the people they monitor, to remain reliable evidence.
questions.pre_read: Treat the footage as audit evidence. Ask which finding could make every recording untrustworthy.
questions.correct_explanation: Camera footage is evidence, and evidence is only useful if the people it might implicate cannot alter it. Guards who can delete footage without approval could remove a record of their own or a colleague's actions, so the whole program loses integrity. Clock drift makes it harder to match footage with badge events, but the recordings still exist and the offset can be corrected.

wrong_explanations.A: Live monitoring at high-risk times is a reasonable, cost-aware design. It is not a weakness on its own.
wrong_explanations.C: Clock drift complicates matching events, but the footage is intact and the offset can be measured and corrected.
wrong_explanations.D: Sixty days is within common retention practice and leaves time to review incidents before footage is overwritten.

tips: Eliminate: A describes sensible targeted monitoring, and D describes a common retention period.
Final two: B beats C because deletable footage destroys the evidence itself, while clock drift only makes it harder to correlate.
Exam cue: when monitoring records are evidence, protecting them from change by the people being monitored outranks convenience issues.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-2 (Physical Access Authorizations); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.2 (Physical Entry)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that every employee badge opens both the office floors and the data center server hall. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Reissue employee badges with a printed photograph
options.B: Lock the server hall outside normal business hours
options.C: Limit server hall access to staff whose roles need it
options.D: Require a PIN with each badge at the server hall door

questions.key_concept: Physical zones should apply least privilege: only staff whose roles require it are authorized for sensitive areas such as server halls.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the problem is proving identity or deciding who may enter at all.
questions.correct_explanation: The weakness is authorization: everyone can enter, whether or not their job requires it. Restricting server hall access to staff with a role-based need applies least privilege and shrinks the number of people who could harm the equipment. Adding a PIN strengthens proof of identity, but every employee would still be allowed in, so the excess access remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Photos help guards spot a borrowed badge, but every employee would still be authorized to enter the server hall.
wrong_explanations.B: Locking after hours leaves every employee with server hall access during the day, when most staff are on site.
wrong_explanations.D: A PIN confirms the badge holder's identity. It does not reduce the number of people allowed into the hall.

tips: Eliminate: A improves badge identification and B narrows the hours; both leave every employee authorized.
Final two: C beats D because the gap is who is allowed in, and a PIN only proves identity for that same oversized group.
Exam cue: separate authentication (proving who you are) from authorization (where you may go); fix the one the stem shows is broken.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-11 (Emergency Power); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.11 (Supporting Utilities); NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 (Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems)
questions.question: During a long utility outage, a data center's only generator will fail within 20 minutes, and failover to the recovery site takes two hours. What should the data center manager do FIRST?

options.A: Shut down database and storage servers in an orderly sequence
options.B: Begin failing over every workload to the recovery site now
options.C: Send customers a written update on the outage status
options.D: Order a portable generator from an equipment rental firm

questions.key_concept: When power loss is imminent and unavoidable, an orderly shutdown protects data integrity; recovery and failover follow.
questions.pre_read: Compare 20 minutes with the two-hour failover. Ask which action protects the data before power drops.
questions.correct_explanation: When power will drop before any alternative is ready, the priority is protecting the data. An orderly shutdown of database and storage servers completes transactions and writes, so nothing is corrupted when the generator stops. Starting failover is the right recovery step, but it cannot finish in 20 minutes, and a transfer cut off midway risks corrupt or inconsistent data at both sites.

wrong_explanations.B: Failover is the recovery plan, but two hours cannot fit into 20 minutes; an interrupted transfer risks inconsistent data at both sites.
wrong_explanations.C: Customer updates matter, but communication does nothing to protect the data before power is lost.
wrong_explanations.D: A rental generator cannot arrive and be connected within 20 minutes, so servers would still lose power abruptly.

tips: Eliminate: C communicates without protecting anything, and D cannot arrive before the generator stops.
Final two: A beats B because an orderly shutdown fits the 20-minute window and protects data integrity, while failover cannot finish in time.
Exam cue: when power loss is certain and imminent, protect data integrity first with a controlled shutdown, then recover.

questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.2 (Physical Entry); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-2 (Physical Access Authorizations); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-3 (Physical Access Control)
questions.question: A contractor entered a restricted server room unescorted on four nights because his cleaning badge also opened that room. Which weakness should the IS auditor report as MOST significant?

options.A: Server room camera footage was reviewed once a month
options.B: The contractor's employer did not vet him properly
options.C: Visitor logs at reception were kept on paper
options.D: Badge rights went beyond the contractor's cleaning role

questions.key_concept: Physical access rights must follow least privilege, so badges open only the areas each role needs.
questions.pre_read: Notice why the contractor could enter. Ask which control should have stopped that badge.
questions.correct_explanation: The contractor could enter because his badge granted access beyond what his cleaning role required, a failure of least privilege in physical access provisioning. Monthly camera review is a weakness too, but it is detective and would only have revealed the visits later; correct badge rights would have prevented them.

wrong_explanations.A: Camera review is detective and would only reveal entries after they happened.
wrong_explanations.B: Vetting reduces insider risk but does not justify server-room access for a cleaner.
wrong_explanations.C: Paper logs at reception do not control which doors a badge opens.

tips: Eliminate: B is about the employer's vetting, and C concerns reception logs, not door access.
Final two: D beats A because correct badge rights prevent entry; camera review only detects it later.
Exam cue: physical access follows least privilege too; badges should open only what the role needs.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-14 (Environmental Controls); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-14(2) (Monitoring with Alarms and Notifications); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.11 (Supporting Utilities)
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews environmental controls for a server room hosting customer databases, where a cooling failure would cause hardware damage within minutes. Which finding is MOST significant?

options.A: Backup cooling covers two-thirds of the peak heat load
options.B: Cooling maintenance records are held by the facilities contractor
options.C: Out-of-hours temperature alarms go to a mailbox nobody monitors
options.D: Humidity readings are reviewed weekly rather than every day

questions.key_concept: Environmental alarms protect information assets only if alerts reach someone who can respond before equipment and data are damaged.
questions.pre_read: Notice damage would follow within minutes. Ask which finding means nobody would know until it was too late.
questions.correct_explanation: Environmental controls exist to protect the systems that hold information. With damage only minutes away, an out-of-hours cooling failure must reach someone who can act; an alarm sent to an unread mailbox means the first sign is failed servers and possible data loss. Partial backup cooling is a real capacity gap, but staff can shed non-critical load to stay within it, provided an alarm reaches them.

wrong_explanations.A: Partial backup cooling is a real gap, but shedding non-critical load can keep critical systems safe if someone is alerted in time.
wrong_explanations.B: Who holds the records is an administrative detail. The auditor can still obtain them to confirm maintenance happens.
wrong_explanations.D: Humidity matters, but weekly review of a slow-changing reading does not stop a temperature alarm reaching anyone.

tips: Eliminate: B concerns where records are kept, and D is a reasonable review interval for a slow-changing reading.
Final two: C beats A because an unseen alarm defeats every response, including the load shedding that offsets partial backup cooling.
Exam cue: a detective control protects nothing unless its alerts reach someone able to respond in time.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev 1 (Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.1 (Physical Security Perimeters)
questions.question: Eight months after an acquisition, the two firms' sites use different badge, visitor and emergency procedures, and no comparison of them exists. What should the IS auditor recommend that management do FIRST?

options.A: Apply the acquirer's stricter standards at every site at once
options.B: Assess each site's current controls and risks before setting targets
options.C: Keep each firm's procedures unchanged to avoid disrupting staff
options.D: Let the audit committee choose the target security standard

questions.key_concept: Post-acquisition security harmonization starts with a current-state and risk assessment, which then drives the target standard and migration priorities.
questions.pre_read: Notice that no comparison of the sites exists yet. Ask what management needs before choosing any target.
questions.correct_explanation: Harmonization needs a baseline. Without knowing each site's controls and risks, management cannot tell which gaps matter most, which sites to fix first, or whether the acquirer's model suits every site. Imposing the stricter standard everywhere sounds safe, but done blind it spreads effort evenly, may disrupt operations, and can miss risks the acquirer's standard never addressed.

wrong_explanations.A: A stricter standard may be the eventual target, but applying it blind skips risk-based prioritization and change planning.
wrong_explanations.C: Leaving divergent procedures in place keeps any weaker site's gaps open with no plan to close them.
wrong_explanations.D: The audit committee oversees; choosing the standard is a management decision. The committee should review the plan, not write it.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves known differences unmanaged, and D gives a management decision to the oversight body.
Final two: B beats A because a current-state assessment must come first; imposing one standard everywhere skips risk-based prioritization.
Exam cue: before standardizing controls, establish the current state and its risks; sometimes the BEST first step is to assess, not act.

questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 5 (Principles relating to processing of personal data); OECD Privacy Guidelines (2013); ISO/IEC 29100:2011 (Privacy framework)
questions.question: A marketing team wants to use customer birth dates, collected solely for age verification, to send birthday offers. Which privacy principle should the data protection officer raise MOST directly?

options.A: Personal data should be used only for the purpose originally stated
options.B: Organizations should collect no more personal data than a purpose needs
options.C: Personal data should be kept accurate and up to date
options.D: Personal data should be protected against unauthorized access or loss

questions.key_concept: Under GDPR Article 5, purpose limitation bars reusing personal data for new purposes incompatible with those stated at collection.
questions.pre_read: Separate how much data was collected from what it is now being used for. Ask which one changed.
questions.correct_explanation: The birth dates were collected for one stated purpose, age verification. Reusing them for marketing is a new purpose the original collection did not cover, which purpose limitation forbids unless the new use is compatible or has its own lawful basis. Data minimization concerns how much was collected; here the amount was justified at collection, so the problem is the reuse, not the volume.

wrong_explanations.B: Minimization concerns collecting no more than needed. The birth dates were needed for age verification, so collecting them was justified.
wrong_explanations.C: Accuracy is not in question; nothing in the stem suggests the birth dates are wrong or out of date.
wrong_explanations.D: Security matters, but no unauthorized access is described. The issue is an authorized team reusing data for a new purpose.

tips: Eliminate: C concerns accuracy and D concerns security; the stem describes neither problem.
Final two: A beats B because the data was legitimately collected, and the issue is reusing it for a new purpose.
Exam cue: when data collected for one reason is wanted for another, think purpose limitation first.
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Canonical privacy principles per GAPP/OECD/GDPR Article 5'. Public sources: GDPR, OECD, AICPA, NIST. No legacy bank citation. questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 15 (Right of Access); GDPR Article 12 (Information and Modalities for Exercise of Rights)
questions.question: A retailer receives an email from someone claiming to be a customer and asking for a copy of all personal data held about her. What should the data protection officer do FIRST?

options.A: Send her the requested data within one month of receiving it
options.B: Charge a standard fee before starting to process it
options.C: Verify the requester's identity before releasing any data
options.D: Refuse unless the request arrives by registered post

questions.key_concept: Data subjects have a right of access, answered within one month, but the controller must confirm identity first to avoid disclosure to impostors.
questions.pre_read: Notice the request came by email from someone claiming to be a customer. Ask what could go wrong if you simply complied.
questions.correct_explanation: Releasing personal data to an impostor would itself be a breach of confidentiality, and an email claim proves nothing. GDPR lets the controller ask for information needed to confirm identity when there is reasonable doubt. Responding within one month is a real obligation, but the deadline serves the genuine customer; meeting it by sending her data to an unverified requester trades one failure for a worse one.

wrong_explanations.A: The one-month deadline is real, but sending data before confirming identity could disclose it to an impostor.
wrong_explanations.B: Access requests are normally free. A fee is allowed for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests, which nothing here suggests.
wrong_explanations.D: Demanding registered post adds a barrier the law does not require; requests can be made by reasonable means, including email.

tips: Eliminate: B charges a fee where access is normally free, and D imposes a form of request the law does not require.
Final two: C beats A because sending data to an unverified requester risks a breach, while verification still fits within the deadline.
Exam cue: before disclosing personal data on request, confirm who is asking; protecting confidentiality comes before speed.
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Data subject rights catalog under GDPR and parallel laws'. Public sources: GDPR, CCPA, LGPD. No legacy bank citation. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-2 (Account Management); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.18 (Access Rights); ISACA Identity and Access Management Audit/Assurance Program
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a clerk who moved from payroll to sales still has payroll access; the quarterly access review is not yet due. What is the MOST likely root cause?

options.A: Access for new hires is granted before their start date
options.B: The quarterly access review is failing to detect excess rights
options.C: Accounts of departed staff are disabled several days late
options.D: Access is not adjusted when staff change roles internally

questions.key_concept: The identity lifecycle has joiner, mover and leaver stages plus periodic recertification; movers must lose old rights when they change roles.
questions.pre_read: Identify which lifecycle stage the clerk passed through. Then check whether the review has had its chance yet.
questions.correct_explanation: The clerk's old rights survived a transfer, which points to the mover process: when someone changes role, old access should be removed as new access is granted. The quarterly review is a detective backstop and may yet catch this, but it is not due yet, so it has not failed. The primary failure is upstream, at the moment of transfer.

wrong_explanations.A: Early provisioning for joiners is a separate issue. The clerk is an existing employee who transferred, not a new hire.
wrong_explanations.B: The review is not yet due, so it has not had a chance to detect this. It is a backstop, not the root cause.
wrong_explanations.C: Late deprovisioning concerns leavers. The clerk is still employed, so the leaver process is not involved.

tips: Eliminate: A concerns joiners and C concerns leavers; the clerk is a mover.
Final two: D beats B because the transfer should have removed the old access, and the review has not yet been due to catch it.
Exam cue: map each access finding to the lifecycle stage that should have prevented it: joiner, mover, leaver or review.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IA-2 (Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users))
questions.question: A bank's CISO must approve a login design for online banking that satisfies a multi-factor authentication requirement. Which proposed design BEST meets it?

options.A: A password followed by a picture-based captcha puzzle to solve
options.B: A password plus a one-time code from a registered phone
options.C: A password plus answers to two personal security questions
options.D: A longer password checked against stricter complexity rules

questions.key_concept: Multi-factor authentication combines factors from different categories (knowledge, possession, inherence); several knowledge checks are still single-factor.
questions.pre_read: Label each element as something you know, have or are. Then count categories, not steps.
questions.correct_explanation: Multi-factor authentication needs factors from different categories: something you know, something you have and something you are. A password plus a code from an app on a registered phone combines knowledge with possession. Security questions add more checks, but they are just more things the user knows, so a password plus questions is still single-factor and falls to the same phishing or data leak.

wrong_explanations.A: A captcha checks that a human is present, not which human. It adds no authentication factor.
wrong_explanations.C: Security questions are another knowledge factor. Two things you know remain one factor category, so this is not multi-factor.
wrong_explanations.D: A stronger password is still one knowledge factor. Complexity improves it but does not add a second category.

tips: Eliminate: A adds a bot check, not an identity factor, and D only strengthens the single password.
Final two: B beats C because a registered phone adds a possession factor, while security questions are just more knowledge.
Exam cue: count factor categories, not checks; multi-factor needs two of know, have and are.
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Canonical MFA factor categories per NIST 800-63B'. Public sources: NIST, FIDO Alliance, ISACA. No legacy bank citation. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 35 (Data Protection Impact Assessment); Article 29 Working Party Guidelines on DPIA (WP248 rev.01, endorsed by the EDPB)
questions.question: A data protection officer reviews four new projects. Which project MOST clearly requires a data protection impact assessment before processing begins?

options.A: Large-scale analysis of patients' health records to profile risk
options.B: Moving employee payroll records onto a new on-premises database server
options.C: An internal wiki holding engineering drawings and documents
options.D: A website redesign that collects no personal data from visitors

questions.key_concept: A data protection impact assessment is required before processing likely to result in high risk, such as large-scale processing of health data.
questions.pre_read: Ask which project involves sensitive data, at scale, used in a new way that could affect people.
questions.correct_explanation: GDPR Article 35 requires a data protection impact assessment when processing is likely to result in high risk to people, and names large-scale processing of special categories such as health data as a trigger. Profiling patients adds to that risk. The payroll move involves personal data, but it is routine processing of the same records for the same purpose, not new high-risk processing.

wrong_explanations.B: Payroll data is personal, but moving it for the same purpose is routine processing and not likely to be high risk by itself.
wrong_explanations.C: Engineering drawings and documents are not personal data about individuals, so the assessment duty does not arise.
wrong_explanations.D: A redesign that collects no personal data involves no personal data processing, so no assessment is needed.

tips: Eliminate: C and D involve no meaningful personal data, so GDPR's assessment duty does not arise.
Final two: A beats B because large-scale health profiling is a named high-risk trigger, while a payroll move is routine processing.
Exam cue: look for high-risk markers such as special category data, large scale, profiling, monitoring or new technology.

questions.framework_ref: GDPR Articles 44-50 (Transfers); Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 (Standard Contractual Clauses); CJEU Schrems II Judgment (C-311/18)
questions.question: A data protection officer learns that EU customer data began flowing yesterday to a US processor with no Data Privacy Framework certification and no signed contractual clauses. What should the officer recommend FIRST?

options.A: Encrypt the data so the transfers can keep running
options.B: Treat the processor's ISO/IEC 27001 certificate as sufficient
options.C: Suspend the transfers until a lawful mechanism exists
options.D: Sign standard contractual clauses while the transfers continue

questions.key_concept: GDPR Chapter V allows transfers outside the EU only on a valid basis such as adequacy, standard contractual clauses or binding corporate rules.
questions.pre_read: Check which legal transfer bases the stem rules out. Then ask whether security measures can replace a legal basis.
questions.correct_explanation: Under GDPR Chapter V, personal data may leave the EU only on a valid basis, such as an adequacy decision, including the Data Privacy Framework for certified US firms, or standard contractual clauses. Neither exists here, so each day's transfer is unlawful and should stop until one is in place. Signing clauses is the right fix, but continuing transfers meanwhile keeps the breach running.

wrong_explanations.A: Encryption is a useful supplementary measure, but it is not a GDPR transfer mechanism and cannot make the transfers lawful.
wrong_explanations.B: ISO/IEC 27001 certifies a security management system. It is not a GDPR transfer mechanism and gives no legal basis for export.
wrong_explanations.D: Clauses are the right remedy, but letting transfers continue until they are signed leaves every transfer in the meantime unlawful.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are security measures, and neither is a legal basis for transferring personal data outside the EU.
Final two: C beats D because transfers without a valid mechanism are unlawful now, so they stop until clauses are signed.
Exam cue: when an activity is unlawful while it runs, the BEST first step is to stop it, then fix the basis.

related_concepts: Data Protection by Design and Default
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 25 (Data Protection by Design and by Default); EDPB Guidelines 4/2019 (Article 25 Data Protection by Design and by Default)
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a new mobile app that shares users' location by default, with an opt-out in its settings. Which recommendation BEST reflects privacy by design?

options.A: Switch location sharing off by default until the user opts in
options.B: Add a clear notice showing users how to switch sharing off
options.C: Encrypt the stored location history using strong, managed keys
options.D: Revisit the default setting after launch if customers complain

questions.key_concept: Privacy by default means the most protective setting applies automatically; users opt in to sharing rather than having to opt out.
questions.pre_read: Notice what happens to a user who never opens the settings. Ask which option protects that user.
questions.correct_explanation: GDPR Article 25 requires data protection by default: the most privacy-protective setting applies without any action by the user. Switching location sharing off until the user opts in fixes the design itself. A clearer opt-out notice improves transparency, another privacy-by-design principle, but users who never read it keep sharing their location.

wrong_explanations.B: A clearer notice helps transparency, but the default still shares location for every user who takes no action, which Article 25 does not allow.
wrong_explanations.C: Encryption protects stored data from outsiders. It does not limit the collection and sharing that the default setting causes.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting for complaints after launch is reactive. Privacy by design anticipates the problem and fixes it before release.

tips: Eliminate: C protects data at rest but leaves the sharing untouched, and D waits for complaints instead of acting before launch.
Final two: A beats B because privacy by default needs no user action; a notice still leaves silent users sharing.
Exam cue: when a stem mentions a default setting, the privacy-by-design answer changes the default, not the explanation of it.
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Privacy by Design seven foundational principles operationalized in GDPR Article 25'. Public sources: GDPR, EDPB, Cavoukian, ISO. questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 7 (Conditions for Consent); GDPR Recital 32; EDPB Guidelines 05/2020 on consent
questions.question: An IS auditor finds the marketing consent box on a retailer's sign-up form is pre-ticked, and each consent is logged with a timestamp. Which concern is MOST significant under GDPR?

options.A: The log may not show which privacy notice version applied
options.B: The consent box sits below the main sign-up button
options.C: A pre-ticked box does not show clear, affirmative agreement
options.D: Consent records are stored without field-level database encryption

questions.key_concept: Valid GDPR consent needs a clear affirmative act; pre-ticked boxes and silence do not count, however well the result is recorded.
questions.pre_read: Notice the box is ticked before the customer acts. Ask whether the customer made any choice at all.
questions.correct_explanation: GDPR requires consent to be a clear affirmative act; silence or a pre-ticked box does not qualify. Every consent captured this way is therefore invalid, and marketing that relies on it has no lawful basis. Recording the notice version supports the controller's Article 7 duty to demonstrate consent, but perfect records cannot rescue consent that was never validly given.

wrong_explanations.A: Article 7 does require the controller to demonstrate consent, but better records of invalid consent still leave the processing without a lawful basis.
wrong_explanations.B: Placement on the page is a design detail. It matters far less than whether the box captures a genuine choice.
wrong_explanations.D: Encrypting the records protects their confidentiality. It does nothing to make the underlying consent valid.

tips: Eliminate: B is a page-layout detail, and D protects stored records without touching whether consent is valid.
Final two: C beats A because a pre-ticked box makes the consent itself invalid; record-keeping only proves consent that was valid to begin with.
Exam cue: fix validity before evidence; if consent was never actively given, no quality of record-keeping can save it.

questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) (Data minimisation); GDPR Article 25 (Data Protection by Design and by Default); ISO/IEC 29100:2011 (Privacy framework)
questions.question: A product owner wants a new onboarding form to also collect date of birth and employer, in case analytics needs them later. What should the IS auditor recommend to BEST support data minimization?

options.A: Mask the extra fields on screens used by support staff
options.B: Collect only the fields needed for a specified, documented purpose
options.C: Seek customer consent to keep the extra fields for analytics
options.D: Keep the extra fields for seven years as audit evidence

questions.key_concept: Data minimization limits collection to what a specified purpose needs; data gathered for an undefined future use should not be collected.
questions.pre_read: Notice the reason given for the extra fields. Ask whether it names any defined purpose.
questions.correct_explanation: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) limits personal data to what is adequate, relevant and necessary for a specified purpose. 'In case analytics needs them' is not a specified purpose, so the extra fields should not be collected. Asking for consent sounds lawful, but consent cannot cover a purpose nobody has defined, and it still enlarges the data the firm must protect.

wrong_explanations.A: Masking limits who sees the fields on screen, but the firm still collects and stores data it has no defined need for.
wrong_explanations.C: Consent must be specific to a defined purpose. A vague future analytics need cannot be meaningfully consented to, and minimization still applies.
wrong_explanations.D: Long retention makes the problem worse. Storage limitation, a sister principle, also requires deleting data once its purpose is served.

tips: Eliminate: A only hides the fields on screen, and D keeps unneeded data even longer.
Final two: B beats C because minimization asks whether data is needed for a defined purpose; consent cannot cover a purpose that does not yet exist.
Exam cue: 'in case we need it later' is the classic minimization failure; the best answer stops the collection rather than protecting or justifying it.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.2 (Privileged Access Rights); CIS Controls v8 Control 6 (Access Control Management)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds domain administrators hold permanent standing rights, protected by hardware-token multi-factor authentication. Which recommendation BEST reduces the remaining risk?

options.A: Vault administrator passwords and rotate them automatically after each use
options.B: Require administrators to sign the acceptable use policy yearly
options.C: Lengthen administrator passwords to at least twenty characters
options.D: Grant administrator rights just in time, with approval and expiry

questions.key_concept: Just-in-time elevation removes standing privilege: rights are granted on approval for a limited time, applying least privilege to time as well as scope.
questions.pre_read: Notice that authentication is already strong. Ask what risk remains when the rights never go away.
questions.correct_explanation: Strong authentication already protects the login, so the remaining exposure is that powerful rights exist all the time, even when no administrative work is under way. Just-in-time elevation applies least privilege to time: rights appear only after approval and expire automatically. Vaulting and rotating passwords protects the credential itself, but the accounts still hold permanent rights for anyone who hijacks a session.

wrong_explanations.A: Vaulting protects the credential, but the accounts keep permanent domain rights that a hijacked session or an insider can use at any time.
wrong_explanations.B: An annual signature is an administrative reminder. It does not reduce how long powerful rights remain available.
wrong_explanations.C: Hardware-token authentication already protects the login. Longer passwords add little and leave the rights permanently available.

tips: Eliminate: B is a paper reminder that changes no rights, and C adds little on top of hardware-token authentication.
Final two: D beats A because removing standing privilege limits misuse at all times, while vaulting only protects the password.
Exam cue: when authentication is already strong, look at how long privilege lasts; least privilege applies to time as well as scope.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63C-4 (Digital Identity Guidelines: Federation and Assertions); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-12 (Session Termination); OpenID Connect Core 1.0 (OpenID Foundation specification)
questions.question: Scoping a federated single sign-on review, an IS auditor learns that users disabled in the identity provider can keep using one SaaS application for hours. What should the auditor examine FIRST?

options.A: The application's session lifetime and how it handles revoked users
options.B: The identity provider's password complexity and lockout settings
options.C: The expiry dates of signing certificates in the federation metadata
options.D: The SaaS vendor's latest assurance report on data centre security

questions.key_concept: In federation, applications keep their own sessions; disabling a user at the identity provider does not end them unless revocation is handled.
questions.pre_read: Notice the users are already disabled centrally. Ask where their continuing access could come from.
questions.correct_explanation: The symptom points to the service provider side of the trust: the application keeps its own session after sign-in and does not recheck the user once the identity provider disables them. Examining session lifetime and revocation handling targets the observed risk directly. Certificate expiry is a genuine federation control, but an expired certificate would stop logins, not let disabled users continue.

wrong_explanations.B: Password settings govern new sign-ins at the identity provider. Disabled users are not signing in again; their old application session carries on.
wrong_explanations.C: Certificate expiry is a real federation risk, but it would break sign-ins rather than let disabled users keep working.
wrong_explanations.D: A data centre assurance report covers the vendor's hosting controls. It does not explain sessions outliving a disabled account.

tips: Eliminate: B concerns new logins at the identity provider, and D covers the vendor's hosting, not user sessions.
Final two: A beats C because the symptom is access that continues after revocation; expired certificates would block logins instead.
Exam cue: let the observed symptom choose the scope; start with the control that could actually produce what the stem describes.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-2 (Account Management); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.2 (Privileged Access Rights)
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a just-in-time access tool that grants elevated rights for four hours at a time. Which finding is MOST significant?

options.A: Four hours exceeds the time most administrative tasks need
options.B: The dashboard does not show elevation trends for each team
options.C: Requesters can approve their own requests for elevated rights
options.D: The request form uses free text rather than structured drop-down lists

questions.key_concept: Just-in-time access depends on independent approval; if requesters approve themselves, time limits alone cannot stop improper elevation.
questions.pre_read: Notice who approves each request. Ask which weakness defeats the control rather than merely loosening it.
questions.correct_explanation: Just-in-time access relies on an independent approver to confirm each elevation is justified. Self-approval removes that check entirely, so anyone with requester rights can grant themselves privilege at will, and the expiry only limits how long each self-granted session lasts. A four-hour window may be longer than needed, but that is tuning within a control that still works.

wrong_explanations.A: A shorter window would tighten least privilege, but the time limit still works. Tuning it matters less than restoring independent approval.
wrong_explanations.B: Missing trend reporting is a management information gap. It does not let anyone obtain privilege improperly.
wrong_explanations.D: Free-text requests make justifications harder to analyze, but they do not remove the approval check.

tips: Eliminate: B is a reporting gap, and D is a form-design detail; neither lets anyone gain privilege improperly.
Final two: C beats A because self-approval removes the control's independent check, while a long window only loosens a control that still functions.
Exam cue: a broken approval step outranks a loose parameter; first ask whether the control's key check still happens at all.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-2 (Account Management); CIS Controls v8 Control 5 (Account Management)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds 300 service accounts with no named owner, though their passwords are vaulted and rotated every 90 days. What should the auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Shorten the vault's rotation interval from ninety to thirty days
options.B: Assign an accountable owner who confirms each account is needed
options.C: Disable the ownerless service accounts immediately to cut exposure
options.D: Convert the service accounts into named interactive user accounts

questions.key_concept: Every service account needs an accountable owner who confirms its purpose and scope, which makes recertification and retirement possible.
questions.pre_read: Notice which control is already working and which is missing. Ask who could decide whether an account is still needed.
questions.correct_explanation: Credential handling is already controlled; the gap is accountability. Without an owner, nobody can confirm what each account does, how much access it needs, or when it should be retired, so recertification and decommissioning cannot happen. Disabling the accounts at once looks decisive, but with no one knowing their purpose it risks breaking production systems that depend on them.

wrong_explanations.A: Credentials are already vaulted and rotated. A shorter interval adds little while the real gap, that nobody is accountable for the accounts, remains.
wrong_explanations.C: Disabling accounts of unknown purpose may stop critical processes and cause outages. Owners must first confirm which accounts are still needed.
wrong_explanations.D: Interactive logins on service accounts increase risk and break automation. Service accounts should stay non-interactive with narrow scope.

tips: Eliminate: A tightens a credential control that already works, and D makes the accounts riskier by allowing interactive logins.
Final two: B beats C because an owner must confirm purpose before access is removed; disabling unknown accounts blindly risks outages.
Exam cue: no owner means no one can decide; when assets lack accountability, assigning ownership comes before reviewing or removing them.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-2 (Account Management); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.18 (Access Rights); ISACA Identity and Access Management Audit/Assurance Program
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that every user's access, including database administrator rights, is recertified once a year by line managers. Which recommendation BEST improves the program?

options.A: Have IT security recertify every account instead of line managers
options.B: Move every account onto a single quarterly review cycle
options.C: Replace the reviews with automated leaver feeds from HR
options.D: Recertify privileged rights quarterly and standard access annually

questions.key_concept: Access recertification should be risk-tiered: privileged rights reviewed more often than standard access, by people who understand the business need.
questions.pre_read: Notice that administrator rights share the same annual cycle as everyone else. Ask where more frequent review earns its cost.
questions.correct_explanation: Review frequency should follow risk. Privileged rights such as database administration can cause the most damage, so they warrant more frequent recertification, while standard access can stay on an annual cycle. Moving every account to quarterly sounds stricter, but it multiplies reviewer workload, encourages rubber-stamping, and spends effort on low-risk access instead of where the exposure is.

wrong_explanations.A: IT security can administer the process, but it cannot judge business need. Managers or data owners should confirm whether access is still required.
wrong_explanations.B: Uniform quarterly reviews raise reviewer fatigue and rubber-stamping, and spend effort on low-risk access rather than focusing on privileged rights.
wrong_explanations.C: Leaver feeds remove departed staff but miss excess access held by current employees, which is what recertification catches.

tips: Eliminate: A gives the decision to a team that cannot judge business need, and C misses excess access held by current staff.
Final two: D beats B because review frequency should follow risk; reviewing everything quarterly breeds rubber-stamping and dilutes attention.
Exam cue: when one rule covers everything, look for the answer that tiers the control by risk rather than tightening it everywhere.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63A-4 (Digital Identity Guidelines: Identity Proofing and Enrollment); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IA-12 (Identity Proofing)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds an online bank verifies new customers using only self-asserted details and knowledge-based questions. Which recommendation BEST strengthens identity proofing?

options.A: Check a government photo ID against a live image of the applicant
options.B: Add more knowledge-based questions drawn from credit bureau files
options.C: Require a stronger password and a one-time code at the first login
options.D: Have applicants accept terms confirming their details are accurate

questions.key_concept: Identity proofing verifies a claimed identity using strong evidence linked to the live applicant; knowledge-based questions give weak assurance.
questions.pre_read: Notice the bank checks only what applicants say about themselves. Ask which option links real evidence to the person applying.
questions.correct_explanation: Identity proofing establishes that the applicant is the real person behind the claimed identity. Validating strong evidence such as a government photo ID and comparing it with a live image of the applicant gives meaningful assurance, as NIST SP 800-63A expects at higher assurance levels. More knowledge-based questions feel thorough, but fraudsters can often obtain the answers from data breaches.

wrong_explanations.B: Knowledge-based answers are frequently exposed in breaches, so more questions add little assurance. NIST guidance treats them as weak evidence of identity.
wrong_explanations.C: Passwords and one-time codes authenticate an account after it exists. They do not prove who opened it.
wrong_explanations.D: A signed declaration is still self-asserted. A fraudster accepts the same terms without hesitation.

tips: Eliminate: C strengthens login rather than proving identity, and D is just another self-asserted claim.
Final two: A beats B because comparing strong evidence with the live applicant proves identity; knowledge-based answers can be bought or stolen.
Exam cue: keep proofing and authentication apart; proofing checks who someone is at enrollment, authentication checks it is the same person later.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management); CISA Fact Sheet on Phishing-Resistant MFA (October 2022); FIDO Alliance FIDO2/WebAuthn Specifications
questions.question: A CISO is choosing multi-factor authentication for cloud administrators, who are frequent targets of credential phishing. Which option BEST meets the need?

options.A: Push approvals sent to each administrator's registered mobile phone
options.B: One-time passcodes delivered to administrators by text message
options.C: Hardware security keys bound to the genuine sign-in site
options.D: Longer passwords combined with stricter account lockout rules

questions.key_concept: Phishing-resistant authenticators such as FIDO2 hardware keys bind the login to the genuine site, so stolen responses cannot be replayed.
questions.pre_read: Notice the threat named in the stem. Ask which factor stays safe if the administrator lands on a fake page.
questions.correct_explanation: Phishing resistance is the deciding need. FIDO2 hardware security keys cryptographically bind the login to the real site, so a fake page cannot relay or reuse the response; NIST SP 800-63B treats such authenticators as phishing-resistant. Push approvals are a genuine second factor, but attackers can relay them through fake sites or wear users down with repeated prompts until one is approved.

wrong_explanations.A: Push approval is a real second factor, but it can be relayed through a phishing site or approved by a tired user after repeated prompts.
wrong_explanations.B: Text-message codes can be phished or intercepted through SIM swapping, and NIST restricts their use as an authenticator.
wrong_explanations.D: This is still a single factor. A phished password works regardless of its length or the lockout settings.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on interceptable text messages, and D is still single-factor authentication.
Final two: C beats A because a hardware key binds to the real site and cannot be relayed, while push approvals can be phished or fatigued.
Exam cue: when the stem names phishing, pick the factor that is cryptographically bound to the site, not just any second step.
