questions.question: A firm keeps only 30 days of security logs in its SIEM because of ingestion costs, although regulation requires one year. Which option should the CISO choose as BEST?

options.A: Formally accept the 30-day retention as a documented risk
options.B: Leave older logs on the systems that generated them
options.C: Filter low-value log sources out before they ever reach the SIEM
options.D: Archive older logs to lower-cost storage that stays searchable

questions.key_concept: Retention duties are met with tiered storage: recent logs in the SIEM for detection, older logs in cheaper searchable storage for the full period.
questions.pre_read: Notice the requirement comes from regulation. Ask which option meets one year of retention at acceptable cost.
questions.correct_explanation: Tiered storage meets the regulatory duty at lower cost: recent logs stay in the SIEM for real-time detection, while older logs move to cheaper, protected storage that investigators can still search for the full year. Filtering sources reduces cost, but it does not extend retention beyond 30 days, and it may discard logs the regulation requires.

wrong_explanations.A: Management cannot accept away a legal retention requirement; risk acceptance applies to discretionary risks, not regulatory obligations.
wrong_explanations.B: Logs left on source systems can be altered or deleted by an attacker and are hard to search in an investigation.
wrong_explanations.C: Filtering trims volume but still keeps only 30 days, and dropped sources may be ones the regulation requires.

tips: Eliminate: A tries to accept a legal duty as a risk, and B leaves logs open to tampering.
Final two: D beats C because only archiving meets the one-year duty; filtering still keeps just 30 days.
Exam cue: when cost conflicts with a retention requirement, look for tiered storage rather than less logging.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-115 (Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CA-5 (Plan of Action and Milestones); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.8 (Management of Technical Vulnerabilities)
questions.question: A penetration tester reports a critical remote code execution flaw in the billing platform, which the contract excluded from testing. What should the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Treat the flaw as a real risk and begin remediation
options.B: Issue a breach-of-contract notice to the testing firm
options.C: Investigate how the tester reached the excluded system
options.D: Reject the finding because the system was out of scope

questions.key_concept: A vulnerability's risk does not depend on how it was found; a critical flaw must be remediated even if found outside the agreed scope.
questions.pre_read: Notice the flaw is critical and real. Ask whether the scope dispute changes the risk to the billing platform.
questions.correct_explanation: Scope governs what testers may do, not whether a vulnerability exists. A critical remote code execution flaw in a billing platform exposes payment data whoever found it, so remediation must start now. How the tester crossed into an excluded system is a fair question for the contract and scope controls, but it can be pursued while the flaw is being fixed.

wrong_explanations.B: A legal notice addresses the vendor relationship, not the exposed billing platform, and does nothing to reduce the risk.
wrong_explanations.C: The scope breach deserves review, but investigating it first leaves a critical, exploitable flaw open in a payment system.
wrong_explanations.D: Rejecting the finding ignores a known critical vulnerability; attackers are not bound by the contract's scope.

tips: Eliminate: D ignores a known critical flaw, and B addresses the contract instead of the risk.
Final two: A beats C because the vulnerability is real now; the scope question can be investigated afterward.
Exam cue: once a critical flaw is known, fix the risk first; how it was discovered is a secondary question.

questions.question: A SaaS firm gathers SOC 2 evidence through ad hoc screenshots, and control failures surface only when the external auditor tests samples. Which improvement should the compliance officer adopt as BEST?

options.A: Monthly control owner attestations tracked in a central register
options.B: Consultants assembling the evidence after the audit period ends
options.C: Automated daily checks of controls mapped to audit criteria
options.D: Extra screenshot collection in the weeks before fieldwork

questions.key_concept: Continuous automated control monitoring finds failures as they happen and produces evidence across the whole period, unlike point-in-time manual collection.
questions.pre_read: Notice failures are found only by the external auditor. Ask which option lets the firm find them first.
questions.correct_explanation: Automated daily checks mapped to each SOC 2 criterion detect a failing control within a day, so it can be fixed before the auditor samples it, and they generate consistent evidence across the whole period. Monthly attestations add structure, but they rely on control owners' own statements and can leave failures unnoticed for weeks.

wrong_explanations.A: Attestations are self-reported and monthly, so failures can persist for weeks and the evidence relies on owners' word.
wrong_explanations.B: Assembling evidence after the period cannot show controls operated during it, and failures stay undetected in real time.
wrong_explanations.D: More screenshots before fieldwork are still point-in-time evidence and cannot show operation across the period.

tips: Eliminate: B builds evidence after the fact, and D adds more of the same point-in-time screenshots.
Final two: C beats A because automated checks find failures daily and independently; attestations are monthly self-reports.
Exam cue: for proving controls operate over a period, prefer continuous automated evidence over periodic self-attestation.

questions.question: A firm stores cardholder and health data across AWS, Azure and GCP but logs only administrative API activity in each cloud. Which gap should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Each provider records events in a different log format
options.B: Access to the stored payment and health records is not logged
options.C: Log storage costs differ between the three providers
options.D: Logs are scattered across each cloud instead of one central store

questions.key_concept: Administrative logs show who changed the cloud; only data-access logs show who read sensitive records, which breach investigations need.
questions.pre_read: Notice which activity is logged. Ask who could read cardholder or health records without leaving any trace.
questions.correct_explanation: Administrative logs show configuration changes, but not who read cardholder or patient records. Without data-access logging, a breach of the most sensitive data leaves no trail, and payment and health data rules both expect access to that data to be recorded. Separate per-cloud stores hamper correlation, but the logs still exist; missing data-access events can never be recovered.

wrong_explanations.A: Format differences are solved by normalizing logs during aggregation and leave no activity unrecorded.
wrong_explanations.C: Cost differences are a budgeting matter, not a gap in the evidence of who accessed sensitive data.
wrong_explanations.D: Decentralized logs slow correlation across clouds, but the events still exist; missing data-access events can never be investigated.

tips: Eliminate: A is solved by normalization, and C is a budget matter, not a control gap.
Final two: B beats D because unlogged access to sensitive records leaves no evidence at all; scattered logs can still be correlated.
Exam cue: missing evidence outranks evidence that is merely inconvenient to use.

questions.question: A rule blocking internet SSH to admin servers was deleted through the cloud console without a change ticket 12 minutes ago, and external connection attempts have begun. What should the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Convene executives to agree a response before any action
options.B: Ask the engineer who made the change about the business need
options.C: Leave the change in place to preserve it as forensic evidence
options.D: Restore the rule immediately from the approved code baseline

questions.key_concept: An unauthorized change that removes a security control under active probing should be reverted at once to the approved baseline, then investigated.
questions.pre_read: Notice the change bypassed change control and attackers are already probing. Ask what closes the exposure fastest.
questions.correct_explanation: The change bypassed change control, removed a preventive control and is already drawing external connection attempts, so the exposure must close now. Restoring the rule from the approved baseline takes minutes and is easily reversed if a legitimate need emerges. Asking the engineer is a fair step, but it keeps admin servers exposed while the engineer is located and questioned.

wrong_explanations.A: Waiting for an executive meeting delays a routine, reversible fix while attackers continue probing.
wrong_explanations.B: Asking first keeps admin servers exposed to live attempts. An unticketed change has no approval, so reverting first is justified.
wrong_explanations.C: Cloud audit logs already record the change, so evidence survives a revert; leaving the port open invites compromise.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps the exposure open for evidence the logs already hold, and A delays a quick, reversible fix.
Final two: D beats B because the change has no approval and attacks have begun; revert first, then ask.
Exam cue: an unauthorized change that removes a security control under live attack is reverted first and investigated after.

questions.question: After an acquisition, a firm runs two SOCs on different SIEM platforms, and the board wants a consolidation plan within five weeks. What should the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Choose the larger SOC's platform and migrate everything within 30 days
options.B: Outsource both SOCs to a provider and retain an oversight role
options.C: Inventory both SOCs' detection rules before choosing a platform
options.D: Keep both SOCs separate indefinitely to avoid disruption

questions.key_concept: Before choosing a consolidated security platform, inventory what each existing SOC detects, so the choice does not silently drop coverage.
questions.pre_read: Notice the five-week window. Ask what must be known before a platform choice can be defended to the board.
questions.correct_explanation: Each SOC holds detection rules and runbooks built for its environment, and choosing a platform blind risks dropping coverage for one estate. Inventorying both rule sets first lets the CISO compare platforms on what they must detect, which fits within the five-week window. Picking the larger SOC's platform is decisive, but size says nothing about which detections would be lost.

wrong_explanations.A: Size does not show which platform covers both environments, and a 30-day migration without inventory risks losing detections.
wrong_explanations.B: Outsourcing is a major strategic choice made without analysis; it does not answer which detections must be preserved.
wrong_explanations.D: Two separate SOCs keep cost and visibility gaps across the merged estate and ignore the board's request.

tips: Eliminate: B makes a strategic leap without analysis, and D ignores the board's consolidation request.
Final two: C beats A because knowing what each SOC detects must come before choosing; size is not coverage.
Exam cue: before a hard-to-reverse platform choice, first establish what each existing setup must keep detecting.

questions.question: A biotech firm with past research theft is designing an insider threat program covering EU staff protected by works councils. Which design should the Chief Security Officer adopt as BEST?

options.A: Tiered monitoring focused on staff who access research data
options.B: Annual awareness training as the program's main control
options.C: Covert monitoring without informing staff or their representatives
options.D: Detailed monitoring of every employee's email and file activity

questions.key_concept: Insider threat monitoring must be proportionate: focus deeper monitoring on roles with access to the most sensitive data, with transparency to staff.
questions.pre_read: Notice both the theft history and the works councils. Ask which design protects research data while staying proportionate.
questions.correct_explanation: The theft history justifies monitoring, but EU employment rules under GDPR Article 88, and works councils, require it to be necessary and proportionate. Focusing deeper monitoring on staff with access to research data protects the crown jewels while limiting intrusion on others. Monitoring every employee's email and files looks thorough, but it is disproportionate, likely unlawful, and floods analysts with low-value alerts.

wrong_explanations.B: Training raises awareness, but it is a weak control against a determined insider and does not detect theft.
wrong_explanations.C: Covert monitoring of EU staff without transparency or consultation breaches employment privacy rules and works council rights.
wrong_explanations.D: Blanket monitoring of all staff is disproportionate under EU employment rules and buries real signals in low-value data.

tips: Eliminate: B cannot detect a determined insider, and C ignores transparency and works council rights.
Final two: A beats D because monitoring must be proportionate; focusing on high-access roles protects data lawfully.
Exam cue: in monitoring questions, prefer the option scaled to data sensitivity over blanket surveillance.

questions.question: To cut SIEM costs, management proposes to stop collecting DNS and endpoint logs, the two largest sources. What should the IS auditor evaluate FIRST?

options.A: Which active detections depend on the DNS and endpoint logs
options.B: Whether cheaper archive storage could hold those logs instead
options.C: Whether peer firms in the sector collect the same sources
options.D: Whether the SIEM vendor supports turning off the two sources

questions.key_concept: Before dropping log sources to save cost, identify the detections that depend on them; archiving keeps history but not live detection.
questions.pre_read: Notice the two sources would be dropped, not stored more cheaply. Ask what the SOC would stop seeing.
questions.correct_explanation: DNS and endpoint logs feed many detections of malware and command-and-control traffic, so dropping them could blind the SOC. The auditor should first establish which active detections and investigations depend on them, since that defines the risk of the cut. Moving the logs to cheaper archive storage sounds like a compromise, but archived logs keep history for investigations and do not feed real-time detection.

wrong_explanations.B: Archiving keeps history for investigations, but archived logs do not feed real-time detection, so the blind-spot risk is still unknown.
wrong_explanations.C: Peer practice shows what others collect, not which of this firm's detections would stop working.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor support shows the change is technically possible; it says nothing about the detection coverage the firm would lose.

tips: Eliminate: C compares with peers instead of this firm's risk, and D asks whether the change is possible, not whether it is safe.
Final two: A beats B because archived logs serve investigations, not live detection; the detection impact must be known first.
Exam cue: before a control or data source is cut for cost, assess what depends on it.

questions.question: Hundreds of a SOC's 900 detection rules reference decommissioned systems, and no rule has a named owner. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep every rule in case the old systems ever return
options.B: Delete the 300 oldest rules to cut the volume
options.C: Assign rule owners and review rules on a set cycle
options.D: Let the SIEM vendor maintain the whole rule set

questions.key_concept: Detection rules need named owners and periodic review so obsolete rules are retired and coverage stays relevant.
questions.pre_read: Notice that no rule has an owner. Ask why the clutter built up in the first place.
questions.correct_explanation: Detection rules decay as the environment changes, so each needs an owner accountable for reviewing it on a set cycle and retiring or updating it. Deleting the oldest rules cuts volume quickly, but age is not relevance: some old rules may guard critical systems, while some new ones already watch retired assets.

wrong_explanations.A: Keeping obsolete rules adds noise and maintenance load with no detection value.
wrong_explanations.B: Rule age does not show relevance; deleting by age may remove needed coverage.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor does not know the firm's systems and cannot own its detection logic.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps known clutter, and D hands firm-specific logic to an outsider.
Final two: C beats B because owned, periodic review targets relevance; deleting by age is arbitrary.
Exam cue: controls without owners decay; assign ownership and a review cycle before cleaning up.

questions.question: A cloud workload alert confirms an attacker running commands on one production container and probing the instance metadata service for cloud credentials. What should the incident manager do FIRST?

options.A: Keep watching the attacker to gather intelligence before acting
options.B: Isolate the compromised container and revoke credentials it could reach
options.C: Rebuild every container in the deployment from a clean image
options.D: Disable the older metadata service version in every cloud account

questions.key_concept: In an active intrusion, contain first: isolate the affected asset and cut off reachable credentials before hardening or rebuilding.
questions.pre_read: The attacker is active right now. Ask which option stops the harm today rather than fixing a weakness for tomorrow.
questions.correct_explanation: An attacker is active and reaching for cloud credentials, so containment comes first. Isolating the container stops further commands and lateral movement, and revoking reachable credentials closes the path to the wider cloud account. Disabling the older metadata service removes one weakness, but it is a hardening step that leaves the live attacker in place and any stolen credentials still valid.

wrong_explanations.A: Observing a live attacker in production lets them move laterally and steal credentials. Containing an active intrusion takes priority.
wrong_explanations.C: Rebuilding everything first destroys forensic evidence before the intrusion is scoped, and it leaves any stolen credentials valid.
wrong_explanations.D: This hardens one weakness but leaves the attacker active in the container and does not invalidate credentials that may already be stolen.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves an active attacker free in production, and C wipes evidence before the intrusion is scoped.
Final two: B beats D because containing the live attacker comes before hardening, and only revocation stops stolen credentials working.
Exam cue: with a confirmed, active intrusion, contain first; eradication and hardening follow once the attacker is cut off.

questions.question: After a breach went undetected for six days, management reports that runtime threat detection now runs on all 47 production services. Which evidence should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: System reports show the detection agent running on every cluster node
options.B: The vendor datasheet lists detection for common container attacks
options.C: Management signed a statement confirming that remediation is complete
options.D: Simulated attacks on sample services raised alerts that analysts handled

questions.key_concept: Evidence of operating effectiveness, such as a test that triggers and handles an alert, outranks evidence that a tool is installed.
questions.pre_read: Recall what failed: no one was alerted for six days. Ask which evidence proves that failure would not happen again.
questions.correct_explanation: The original failure was that an attack produced no alert anyone acted on. Only a test showing that attack behaviour triggers alerts which reach analysts and are handled proves the control operates end to end. Agent status reports show the tool is installed and running, but not that its detections fire or that alerts are routed and worked.

wrong_explanations.A: This shows installation and coverage, not that rules detect attacks or that alerts reach analysts. Running agents can still produce no actionable alert.
wrong_explanations.B: A vendor's general claim says nothing about this organization's configuration, rule set or alert routing.
wrong_explanations.C: A management assertion is weak evidence on its own. The auditor needs independent evidence that the control actually works.

tips: Eliminate: B is a generic vendor claim, and C is a management assertion rather than independent evidence.
Final two: D beats A because alerts raised and handled prove the control operates, while agent status proves only that it is installed.
Exam cue: when asked whether a gap is closed, prefer evidence that the control worked end to end over evidence that it exists.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews an incident response plan that covers preparation, detection, containment and recovery in detail. Which omission should concern the auditor MOST?

options.A: No rule to issue a press release for every incident
options.B: No step feeds lessons learned back into controls and the plan
options.C: No requirement to file a final report when each incident closes
options.D: No scripted procedure for every possible type of attack

questions.key_concept: Incident response is a cycle: post-incident lessons learned must feed back into controls, playbooks and preparation.
questions.pre_read: List the phases the stem names, then ask which phase of the incident response lifecycle is missing.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan covers every phase except post-incident activity, so the organization responds but never improves. A lessons-learned step turns each incident into fixes for controls, playbooks and training, closing the response lifecycle. A closing report documents what happened, but documentation without a feedback loop lets the same weaknesses cause the next incident.

wrong_explanations.A: Public statements depend on severity and legal advice. A blanket press release rule is neither required nor sensible.
wrong_explanations.C: A report records the incident but does not by itself drive changes to controls or the plan. Learning, not paperwork, completes the lifecycle.
wrong_explanations.D: Scripting every possible attack is unworkable. Good plans use a framework with playbooks for the most likely scenarios.

tips: Eliminate: D asks for impossible exhaustive scripts, and A demands publicity regardless of severity or legal advice.
Final two: B beats C because the missing phase is about improving controls, and a report alone records without improving anything.
Exam cue: the incident lifecycle ends with lessons learned feeding back into preparation; a plan that stops at recovery never gets better.

questions.question: An IS auditor begins evaluating an organization's incident response plan. What should the auditor review FIRST?

options.A: Whether management approved it and aligned it with security policy
options.B: Whether monitoring tools run the latest software versions
options.C: Whether each past incident has its own separate written procedure
options.D: Whether playbooks exist for the most likely attack scenarios

questions.key_concept: An auditor first confirms a plan is approved by management and aligned with policy and risk, then evaluates its detailed procedures.
questions.pre_read: The word FIRST asks about sequence. Ask what must be true before the plan's detail is worth testing.
questions.correct_explanation: A plan carries authority only if management has approved it and it fits the security policy and risk assessment that define what must be protected. Checking this first confirms the plan is the right baseline before testing its detail. Playbooks matter, but reviewing them first risks assessing procedures that management never endorsed or that miss the organization's priorities.

wrong_explanations.B: Tool versions are a technical detail, not a test of whether the plan is governed and fit for purpose.
wrong_explanations.C: A procedure for each past incident creates an unmanageable plan and ignores new threats. Plans rely on a framework and playbooks instead.
wrong_explanations.D: Playbook review is a later step. Without approval and policy alignment, the auditor may assess procedures that lack authority or miss key risks.

tips: Eliminate: B checks technology before governance, and C rewards an unwieldy procedure-per-incident approach.
Final two: A beats D because the plan's authority and fit with policy must be confirmed before its detailed procedures are evaluated.
Exam cue: when an auditor reviews any plan FIRST, start with approval and alignment to policy, then examine the detail.

questions.question: At a mid-sized firm, one security operations analyst runs every incident end to end, including legal liaison and executive updates. Which change would BEST strengthen incident response?

options.A: Hire a second experienced analyst to share the technical and reporting workload
options.B: Require executive approval before any containment step is taken
options.C: Let each business unit head run incidents in their own area
options.D: Name an incident commander and assign legal and communications roles

questions.key_concept: An effective incident response team has a coordinating incident commander and defined roles for technical, legal and communication work.
questions.pre_read: Notice how many different duties one analyst carries. Ask whether the problem is capacity or structure.
questions.correct_explanation: The weakness is structural: one person holds technical, legal and communication duties with no defined authority or specialist input. Naming an incident commander and assigning legal and communications roles gives clear decision authority and the right expertise. A second analyst eases the workload, but technical staff would still be making legal and executive decisions without a defined structure.

wrong_explanations.A: More capacity helps, but legal, communications and decision authority would still sit with technical staff, and no one would coordinate the response.
wrong_explanations.B: An approval gate before every containment step slows response when speed limits damage. Containment authority belongs with the incident lead.
wrong_explanations.C: Splitting incidents by business area fragments coordination. Incidents cross boundaries and need a single coordinating role.

tips: Eliminate: B slows containment with an approval gate, and C splits incidents across business units with no coordinator.
Final two: D beats A because the gap is missing roles and authority, not just analyst capacity.
Exam cue: when one person carries every incident duty, look for the answer that defines roles and authority, not one that adds headcount.

questions.question: A firm ranks incident severity solely by the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score of the exploited flaw. Which weakness should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Scores cannot be produced quickly enough during triage
options.B: Different analysts may score the same vulnerability in different ways
options.C: Incidents exposing sensitive data may receive too low a priority
options.D: Severity ratings will be too detailed for executives to read

questions.key_concept: Incident severity should reflect business impact and data classification, not only the technical score of the exploited flaw.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a vulnerability score leaves out. Picture a low-scoring flaw that exposes highly sensitive data.
questions.correct_explanation: Technical severity ignores what was affected. A low-scoring flaw that exposes regulated personal data can matter far more than a critical flaw on an isolated test server. Severity must reflect business impact and data classification so that response effort follows the value of the asset. Inconsistent scoring is a real quality concern, but even perfectly consistent scores would still misrank incidents.

wrong_explanations.A: Published vulnerability scores are usually available quickly. Speed is not the reason this approach fails.
wrong_explanations.B: Scoring consistency matters, but consistent technical scores would still ignore data sensitivity and business impact.
wrong_explanations.D: Readability for executives is a presentation issue, not a weakness in how incident risk is prioritized.

tips: Eliminate: D is a presentation issue, and A misjudges speed, since published scores are quick to obtain.
Final two: C beats B because ignoring data classification misranks incidents even when every score is applied consistently.
Exam cue: priority should follow the value and classification of the asset affected, not a technical score alone.

questions.question: An incident procedure escalates to the CISO only if an analyst rates the incident critical at triage. Which improvement is MOST important?

options.A: Escalate automatically when containment misses its target time
options.B: Escalate every incident directly to the chief executive
options.C: Let analysts escalate whenever they personally see fit
options.D: Add a second analyst to independently review each triage rating

questions.key_concept: Escalation needs several triggers, including time and impact, so incidents that worsen after triage still reach decision-makers.
questions.pre_read: Notice that escalation happens only once, at triage. Ask what happens to an incident that gets worse afterwards.
questions.correct_explanation: The procedure's single trigger is a one-time judgement at triage, so an incident that worsens or drags on never reaches leadership. Adding time-based and impact-based triggers, such as missed containment targets, makes escalation follow how the incident develops. A second review improves the initial rating, but still relies on that one moment and misses later deterioration.

wrong_explanations.B: Sending every incident to the chief executive overwhelms leadership and blurs priorities. Escalation should be selective and criteria-based.
wrong_explanations.C: Removing criteria makes escalation inconsistent and personal. Clear, defined triggers are the point of an escalation procedure.
wrong_explanations.D: A second reviewer improves the triage rating but still depends on that single moment. Incidents that worsen later would still never escalate.

tips: Eliminate: B floods the chief executive with every incident, and C removes criteria and makes escalation inconsistent.
Final two: A beats D because a better triage rating still misses incidents that worsen after triage; a time trigger catches them.
Exam cue: good escalation has several triggers, including time and impact, not one judgement made at the start.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-84 (Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities); FEMA Homeland Security Exercise and Evaluation Program (HSEEP); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IR-3 (Incident Response Testing)
questions.question: An IS auditor notes that the annual incident tabletop exercise has reused the same generic ransomware scenario and participants for four years. What should the auditor recommend MOST strongly?

options.A: Add more business departments to the existing exercise
options.B: Replace tabletop exercises with unannounced attacks on production
options.C: Keep the script fixed so that yearly scores can be compared
options.D: Base scenarios on current threats and rotate the participants each year

questions.key_concept: Exercises must reflect the organization's current threats and change over time; a repeated script tests memory, not readiness.
questions.pre_read: Find the root of the finding: the same scenario, year after year. Ask which option actually changes that.
questions.correct_explanation: A repeated, generic scenario tests memory rather than readiness and leaves the firm's real threats unexercised. Building scenarios from the current threat profile, with fresh injects and rotating participants, exposes gaps people have not rehearsed. Widening attendance is worthwhile, but more people rehearsing the same familiar script will still not reveal weaknesses against the threats the firm actually faces.

wrong_explanations.A: Broader attendance helps, but everyone would still rehearse the same stale scenario, so gaps against current threats stay hidden.
wrong_explanations.B: Unannounced attacks on production risk real outages. Tabletops are a safe, essential step and should be improved, not dropped.
wrong_explanations.C: A fixed script is exactly the weakness found. Comparable scores mean little if the scenario no longer reflects real threats.

tips: Eliminate: B drops a safe test for risky production attacks, and C keeps the very script that caused the finding.
Final two: D beats A because the weakness is a stale scenario, and more attendees rehearsing it will not expose new gaps.
Exam cue: an exercise that never changes tests memory, not readiness; prefer scenarios drawn from current threats.

questions.question: Management plans to choose an outside incident response provider through competitive bidding only after a major incident occurs. Which recommendation should the IS auditor make FIRST?

options.A: Approve an emergency budget so that bids can be evaluated faster
options.B: Agree a retainer with defined response times before any incident
options.C: Keep a shortlist of prequalified incident responders to call when needed
options.D: Train help desk staff to perform forensic investigations

questions.key_concept: Arrange external incident response support in advance, with contracted response times and terms, so that help can start immediately.
questions.pre_read: Notice when the provider would be chosen. Ask what that delay costs once an attacker is active.
questions.correct_explanation: Buying help during an incident costs hours or days while the attacker remains active, and terms such as scope, confidentiality and evidence handling get negotiated under pressure. A retainer agreed in advance fixes response times, scope and legal terms so experts can start at once. A shortlist saves search time, but without a signed contract the firm still negotiates and has no guaranteed response.

wrong_explanations.A: Faster bidding is still bidding during an incident. Delay and rushed contract terms remain.
wrong_explanations.C: A shortlist saves search time, but without a signed agreement there is no guaranteed response time and terms are still negotiated mid-incident.
wrong_explanations.D: Forensic work needs specialist skills and tools. Untrained help desk staff can damage evidence and miss the attacker.

tips: Eliminate: D gives specialist forensics to untrained staff, and A only speeds up a bidding process that should not happen mid-incident.
Final two: B beats C because only a signed retainer guarantees response times and settled terms before the attack starts.
Exam cue: arrange critical external help before an incident; anything negotiated during the crisis costs time you do not have.

questions.question: During past incidents, executives drafted customer and public statements from scratch, and legal counsel reviewed none of them. Which control should management adopt to BEST address this?

options.A: No external communication until the incident is fully resolved
options.B: The same full technical report sent to each audience
options.C: Pre-approved message templates for each audience, with legal review
options.D: One designated and media-trained spokesperson for every public statement

questions.key_concept: Prepare incident messages in advance: audience-specific templates with legal approval reduce errors and liability under pressure.
questions.pre_read: Name both weaknesses in the stem: who drafts, and who reviews. Ask which option fixes both.
questions.correct_explanation: The weaknesses are improvised content and no legal check, which risk inaccurate statements, missed regulatory requirements and admissions that create liability. Templates prepared for each audience and pre-approved by legal fix both problems before an incident starts. A single spokesperson gives a consistent voice, but that person would still be improvising unreviewed messages under pressure.

wrong_explanations.A: Silence until resolution leaves customers uninformed and can breach notification duties. It does not fix unreviewed messaging.
wrong_explanations.B: One technical report for everyone may disclose sensitive detail and confuse non-technical readers. Messages should suit each audience.
wrong_explanations.D: A spokesperson gives one consistent voice, but the content would still be drafted under pressure without legal review.

tips: Eliminate: A replaces bad messages with silence, and B overshares technical detail to every audience.
Final two: C beats D because the gaps are improvised content and no legal review, which a spokesperson alone does not fix.
Exam cue: prepare and approve incident messages before the crisis; under pressure, people improvise and mistakes follow.

questions.question: During an active incident, the CISO wants to share attack indicators with an industry information sharing group. What should the CISO confirm FIRST?

options.A: Indicators carry sharing labels and exclude customer personal data
options.B: Every member of the group has signed a binding nondisclosure agreement
options.C: The attack has been attributed to a named threat actor
options.D: The incident has been fully closed and formally reviewed

questions.key_concept: Share threat indicators early but safely: strip personal data and label each item with handling limits such as Traffic Light Protocol.
questions.pre_read: Think about what the shared package itself contains. Ask which safeguard the CISO directly controls.
questions.correct_explanation: Sharing indicators helps peers defend themselves, but the shared data must not become a disclosure itself. Removing customer personal data and labelling indicators with sharing limits, such as Traffic Light Protocol markings, protects confidentiality and controls onward distribution. Member agreements add a contractual layer, but they do not keep personal data out of the package or set limits on each item shared.

wrong_explanations.B: Agreements help, but they do not keep personal data out of what is shared or tell recipients how far each item may spread.
wrong_explanations.C: Indicators are useful without attribution. Waiting for it delays warnings that could protect other organizations now.
wrong_explanations.D: Indicators lose value quickly. Sharing early, with proper safeguards, is how peers benefit during an active campaign.

tips: Eliminate: C waits for attribution that indicators do not need, and D delays sharing until the indicators have lost their value.
Final two: A beats B because the CISO controls what leaves the firm; agreements cannot stop personal data being sent in the first place.
Exam cue: when sharing security data externally, protect what is in the package first, then rely on agreements.

questions.question: After each major incident, a firm's post-incident review names the employee at fault and records disciplinary action. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Named employees may need extra security awareness training
options.B: Disciplinary records may breach employee privacy rules
options.C: Review reports may be too long for executives to read
options.D: Staff may hide mistakes, so root causes go unreported

questions.key_concept: Post-incident reviews should be blameless and focus on systems and root causes; blame drives concealment and repeat incidents.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a review is for. Then ask what naming and disciplining people does to honest reporting.
questions.correct_explanation: A blame-focused review discourages people from admitting errors or describing what really happened, so process and control weaknesses stay hidden and incidents recur. Reviews should focus on systems and contributing factors so root causes surface and get fixed. Privacy handling of disciplinary records deserves attention, but it is secondary to a review design that defeats the review's purpose.

wrong_explanations.A: Training may help an individual, but it does not address the concealment that blame creates across the whole team.
wrong_explanations.B: Privacy of disciplinary records is a valid point, but it is secondary to a review design that stops root causes from being found.
wrong_explanations.C: Report length is a presentation issue and does not affect whether the review finds and fixes root causes.

tips: Eliminate: C is a presentation issue, and A treats one person's training as the fix for a team-wide problem.
Final two: D beats B because blame defeats the review's purpose of finding root causes, while record privacy is a narrower handling issue.
Exam cue: post-incident reviews exist to find root causes; anything that discourages honest disclosure undermines them.

questions.question: Ransomware hits a firm's US and EU cloud regions at the same time, and each region has its own response retainer. What should the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Let the US team decide and notify every regulator centrally
options.B: Appoint one incident commander to coordinate both regional teams
options.C: Delay containment until both retainers agree a joint plan
options.D: Run separate regional responses, each led by its own local commander

questions.key_concept: A single incident across several regions needs one incident commander, while regional teams handle local evidence and notification duties.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether this is one incident or two. Then ask who should decide for it.
questions.correct_explanation: One attack across two regions needs one decision-maker, so containment, evidence and messages stay consistent and findings move quickly between teams. A single incident commander can still use each region's retainer and meet each jurisdiction's notification rules. Separate regional responses respect local rules, but they risk conflicting actions and miss links between related attacks.

wrong_explanations.A: One region cannot meet every jurisdiction's notification duties alone. EU notifications follow EU rules and timelines.
wrong_explanations.C: Delaying containment for agreement lets the ransomware spread. Containment proceeds while the joint plan is formed.
wrong_explanations.D: Regional autonomy respects local rules but risks conflicting containment, inconsistent messages and missed links between attacks that are likely related.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores each jurisdiction's own notification rules, and C lets ransomware spread while teams negotiate.
Final two: B beats D because one attack needs one decision-maker, while regional teams still handle local evidence and notices.
Exam cue: one incident in many places needs one commander; local teams execute, but decisions are coordinated.

questions.question: During a confirmed ransomware attack, a manager proposes pausing containment until the cyber insurer approves responders, since the policy covers losses. What should the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Pause containment until the insurer approves its panel responders
options.B: Pay the ransom quickly and seek reimbursement from the insurer
options.C: Continue containment now and notify the insurer in parallel
options.D: Claim the full policy limit before any losses are known

questions.key_concept: Cyber insurance transfers financial loss, not the duty to protect information; continue containment while notifying the insurer promptly.
questions.pre_read: Notice the attack is still active. Ask whether an insurance policy changes the duty to protect the data right now.
questions.correct_explanation: Insurance transfers part of the financial loss, but it does not transfer the duty to protect the firm's data and systems. Containment must continue while the insurer is notified promptly, so coverage conditions are met without letting the ransomware spread. Waiting for insurer-approved responders sounds like protecting coverage, but every hour of delay lets more data be encrypted or stolen, and policies expect the insured to limit loss.

wrong_explanations.A: Policies expect the insured to limit loss. Halting containment for approvals lets the attack spread and damages more data.
wrong_explanations.B: Paying without insurer, legal and sanctions checks can void cover and break the law, and payment does not guarantee recovery.
wrong_explanations.D: Claims must reflect actual losses. Claiming the limit before costs are known misrepresents the loss and damages the relationship with the insurer.

tips: Eliminate: B pays without legal or insurer checks, and D claims the limit before any loss is known.
Final two: C beats A because insurance shifts financial loss, not the duty to protect data; containment cannot wait for approvals.
Exam cue: insurance transfers money risk, never the duty to protect; keep protecting the asset while you notify.

questions.subtopic: SaaS Customer Material Data Breach. Notification First
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 33 (Notification of Personal Data Breach to Supervisory Authority); GDPR Article 28 (Processor obligations); HIPAA Breach Notification Rule (45 CFR §§ 164.400-414)
questions.question: A cloud service provider has contained a breach and confirmed which 47 business customers' personal data was exposed; those customers face their own regulatory deadlines. What should management do FIRST?

options.A: Notify the affected customers now with the confirmed facts
options.B: Issue a public press release before contacting affected customers
options.C: Finish the forensic investigation before contacting any customer
options.D: File breach reports with each customer's regulator on their behalf

questions.key_concept: A provider that confirms a breach of customer data should notify the affected customers promptly so they can meet their own obligations.
questions.pre_read: Notice what is already confirmed and whose deadlines are running. Ask who needs to know first.
questions.correct_explanation: The 47 customers control the exposed data and face their own regulatory deadlines, which they cannot meet until they are told. Notifying them now with the confirmed facts, and updating them as forensics finishes, lets them act in time. Completing the investigation first sounds careful, but the deciding facts are already confirmed, and waiting could make customers miss their deadlines.

wrong_explanations.B: Customers should not learn of a breach of their data from the press. Direct notice to those affected comes first.
wrong_explanations.C: The key facts are already confirmed. Waiting for complete forensics can make customers miss their own regulatory deadlines.
wrong_explanations.D: The customers control the data and their regulatory duties. The provider supports them but should not file on their behalf.

tips: Eliminate: D takes over duties that belong to the customers, and B lets customers learn of the breach from the press.
Final two: A beats C because the affected customers are known and their deadlines are running; full forensics can follow as updates.
Exam cue: when others' legal deadlines depend on your notice, notify with confirmed facts and update later.
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'B2B SaaS material customer data breach — customer notification first action'. Public sources: ISACA, SEC, HIPAA, GDPR, ABA. No legacy bank citation. NEW single-focus principle: NOTIFY-FIRST-FOR-CUSTOMER-PROTECTION. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 33 (Notification of Personal Data Breach to Supervisory Authority); HIPAA Breach Notification Rule (45 CFR §§ 164.400-414); SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05 (Cybersecurity Disclosure Rule, December 2023)
questions.question: A healthcare technology firm's breach triggers notification duties to nine regulators, each with a different deadline. What should management ensure FIRST?

options.A: The strictest regulator is notified on behalf of the others
options.B: Notifications wait until the full scope is confirmed
options.C: Regulators are notified one at a time, strictest deadline first
options.D: Every regulator's deadline is mapped and notices proceed in parallel

questions.key_concept: When an incident triggers several regulators, map every notification duty and deadline and run the notifications in parallel.
questions.pre_read: Notice the nine different deadlines. Ask whether they run one after another or all at once.
questions.correct_explanation: Each regulator's clock runs independently, so a single sequence or a delay puts later deadlines at risk. Mapping every obligation and running notifications in parallel, coordinated by counsel for consistent facts, meets each deadline. Handling the strictest regulator first looks like sensible prioritization, but working one regulator at a time can still let the other deadlines lapse.

wrong_explanations.A: Notifying one regulator does not satisfy the others. Each has its own legal duty and deadline.
wrong_explanations.B: Regulatory clocks keep running during the investigation. Initial notices with known facts can be followed by updates.
wrong_explanations.C: Prioritizing by deadline sounds sensible, but working one regulator at a time can let the other clocks run out.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes one regulator covers the rest, and B lets every clock run while waiting for full scope.
Final two: D beats C because deadlines run at the same time, so a strict sequence can still miss later ones.
Exam cue: several legal clocks running at once call for a mapped, parallel response, not a queue.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 (Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management); ISO 22361:2022 (Security and Resilience — Crisis Management — Guidelines); DRII Professional Practice 9 (Crisis Communications)
questions.question: Six hours into a ransomware outage, customers face visible service failures, call volumes have surged and a reporter has asked for comment. What should management do FIRST about communication?

options.A: Issue a holding statement to investors before updating customers
options.B: Update affected customers regularly on impact and next steps
options.C: Stay silent publicly until every system is fully restored
options.D: Publish full technical details of the attack to everyone

questions.key_concept: During a visible incident, give affected customers timely, factual and regular updates; silence and over-disclosure both cause harm.
questions.pre_read: Ask who is affected right now and what they need to know.
questions.correct_explanation: Customers are already living with the outage, and silence fills with speculation and floods support lines. Regular, factual updates on what is affected and what is being done maintain trust without disclosing sensitive detail. Investor communication matters and may be required, but customers are the audience being harmed now, and briefing investors first while customers wait damages trust further.

wrong_explanations.A: Investor communication may be required, but customers are being harmed now. Leaving them uninformed while investors are briefed erodes trust.
wrong_explanations.C: Silence during a visible outage fuels speculation and overwhelms support. Customers need timely, factual updates.
wrong_explanations.D: Full technical detail can help attackers and confuse customers. Updates should be factual but appropriate to each audience.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves customers guessing during a visible outage, and D overshares detail that can help attackers.
Final two: B beats A because customers are the audience being harmed right now; investors matter but are not first.
Exam cue: in a visible incident, communicate first with those directly affected, factually and regularly.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IR-3 (Incident Response Testing); NIST SP 800-84 (Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities); NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 (Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management)
questions.question: After a tabletop exercise exposed unclear escalation and missing playbooks, the CISO revised the incident response plan. What is the BEST next step?

options.A: Close the exercise findings because the plan was edited
options.B: Present the revised plan to the board for approval
options.C: Validate the revised plan in a follow-up exercise
options.D: Replace the plan with an unmodified vendor template

questions.key_concept: After revising a plan, retest it to confirm the gaps are closed before seeking approval or closing the findings.
questions.pre_read: Ask what proves the revised plan works. Editing the text is not evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: Editing a plan does not prove the gaps are fixed. A follow-up exercise shows whether escalation now works and the new playbooks are usable, so leaders approve a plan known to work. Board approval matters, but seeking it before validation gives the board false assurance about a plan whose fixes have not been tested.

wrong_explanations.A: A finding is closed when the fix is shown to work, not when a document is edited.
wrong_explanations.B: Approval is needed, but approving an untested revision gives false assurance. Validation should come first.
wrong_explanations.D: A generic template ignores the organization's own systems, roles and regulators, and was not what the exercise tested.

tips: Eliminate: D discards the firm's own plan for a generic one, and A closes findings without proving the fixes work.
Final two: C beats B because the board should approve a plan shown to work, not a revision that is still untested.
Exam cue: after a fix, verify it before you report it closed or seek approval.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 (Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.26 (Response to Information Security Incidents)
questions.question: A defense contractor finds a nation-state group still active in its engineering network, and its communications team wants to publish the technical findings today. What should management do FIRST?

options.A: Hold the public release until a coordinated eradication is ready
options.B: Publish the findings today to warn other defense contractors
options.C: Adopt a standing policy against publishing threat findings
options.D: Remove the attacker's access from each system as it is found

questions.key_concept: While an advanced attacker remains in the network, avoid tipping it off; publish findings and evict it in one coordinated step.
questions.pre_read: Notice the attacker is still active in the network. Ask what a public report today would tell it.
questions.correct_explanation: The attacker is still inside, and a public report tells it exactly what defenders have found, so it can switch to hidden footholds or take more data. Holding the release until a coordinated eradication is ready protects the information assets; required reports to authorities continue meanwhile. Removing access system by system feels proactive, but it also alerts the attacker, who keeps the footholds not yet found.

wrong_explanations.B: Publishing while the attacker is inside reveals what defenders know, so it can hide, change tools or steal more first.
wrong_explanations.C: A blanket ban ignores the value of sharing findings once the threat is removed. Timing, not secrecy, is the issue.
wrong_explanations.D: Piecemeal removal warns the attacker, who then relies on footholds not yet found. Eviction should happen in one coordinated step.

tips: Eliminate: B tips off an attacker still inside, and C bans sharing even after the threat is removed.
Final two: A beats D because coordinated eradication removes every foothold at once; piecemeal removal warns the attacker first.
Exam cue: while an advanced attacker is still inside, avoid any step that reveals what you know until you can evict it completely.

questions.subtopic: Major Architecture Decision During Active Incident
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 (Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.26 (Response to Information Security Incidents); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.27 (Learning from Information Security Incidents)
questions.question: At hour 18 of an unresolved ransomware incident, an executive asks the response team to begin migrating affected systems to a new cloud platform immediately. What is the incident manager's BEST response?

options.A: Start the migration now so restored systems run on the new platform
options.B: Defer the migration until the intrusion is eradicated and reviewed
options.C: Reject the migration because it was proposed once before
options.D: Let the executive approve the migration under emergency powers

questions.key_concept: Do not migrate or rebuild during an unresolved intrusion; eradicate first, or the attacker's tools and access move into the new environment.
questions.pre_read: Notice the intrusion is not yet resolved. Ask what would travel with the systems if they moved now.
questions.correct_explanation: The intrusion is not yet scoped or eradicated, so systems moved now may carry the attacker's tools and access into the new platform, spreading the compromise to a clean environment. Deferring the migration until eradication is complete and the post-incident review shows the root cause keeps responders focused and protects the new platform. Migrating now feels like progress, but it risks rebuilding on infected systems.

wrong_explanations.A: Moving unscoped systems can carry the attacker's tools into the new platform and pulls responders away from containment.
wrong_explanations.C: An earlier proposal is no reason to reject. The migration deserves proper review once the intrusion is removed.
wrong_explanations.D: Emergency powers exist for urgent response actions, not platform moves. Using them here bypasses both governance and the response plan.

tips: Eliminate: C rejects for a reason unrelated to merit, and D misuses emergency powers to bypass governance.
Final two: B beats A because moving systems before eradication can carry the attacker into the new platform.
Exam cue: never rebuild or migrate until the intrusion is scoped and eradicated; otherwise the attacker moves with you.

questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 28 (Processor obligations); GDPR Article 33 (Notification of Personal Data Breach to Supervisory Authority); COBIT 2019 APO10 (Managed Vendors)
questions.question: A payroll vendor reports a breach that may expose employees' bank and identity data and promises formal notice within 72 hours. What should the firm's CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Move the employee data to a new vendor during the incident
options.B: Tell employees now that their data has been stolen
options.C: Wait for the vendor's formal notice, since the vendor owns the breach
options.D: Engage the vendor now to confirm which employee data was exposed

questions.key_concept: Outsourcing processing does not outsource accountability: after a vendor breach, the firm must act at once to establish its own exposure.
questions.pre_read: Notice who owns the employee data. Ask what that owner must know before deciding on notices.
questions.correct_explanation: The firm remains accountable for its employees' data even when a vendor processes it. Engaging the vendor immediately establishes what was exposed, so the firm can assess its own notification duties and protective steps such as credit monitoring. Telling employees at once feels transparent, but announcing unconfirmed theft can mislead them; accurate, prompt notice follows confirmation.

wrong_explanations.A: Moving data mid-incident adds risk and does not establish what was already exposed.
wrong_explanations.B: Announcing theft before exposure is confirmed can mislead staff and may need correcting. Prompt, accurate notice follows confirmation.
wrong_explanations.C: Outsourcing processing does not transfer accountability. The firm must act now to understand its own exposure and duties.

tips: Eliminate: C passes accountability to the vendor, and A moves data mid-incident without learning what was exposed.
Final two: D beats B because the firm must confirm what was exposed before telling employees their data was stolen.
Exam cue: outsourcing a process never outsources accountability for the data; the owner acts first.

questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1402 (Follow-up Activities); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CA-5 (Plan of Action and Milestones)
questions.question: An external assessment of incident readiness reports three critical, seven high and eight medium findings. Which remediation approach should management adopt as BEST?

options.A: Outsource the program and its accountability to a vendor
options.B: Adopt a vendor template in place of current procedures
options.C: Set owners and risk-based deadlines for every finding
options.D: Fix the critical findings and defer the others to next year

questions.key_concept: Remediate findings by risk: give every finding an owner and a deadline, with tighter deadlines for higher severity.
questions.pre_read: Count the severities in the stem. Ask what happens to the high findings under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk-based remediation gives every finding an owner and a deadline scaled to its severity, so critical gaps are fixed fastest while high and medium ones are not forgotten. Fixing only the critical items is a reasonable start, but deferring seven high-risk findings for a year leaves known serious exposures open with no plan, which management should not accept by default.

wrong_explanations.A: Services can be outsourced, but accountability for incident readiness stays with management.
wrong_explanations.B: A generic template does not fix the specific gaps found and ignores the firm's own systems and obligations.
wrong_explanations.D: Starting with critical findings is right, but deferring seven high findings for a year leaves serious known risks open with no owner or plan.

tips: Eliminate: A tries to outsource accountability, and B swaps in a generic template that ignores the actual findings.
Final two: C beats D because every finding needs an owner and a deadline, with the tightest deadlines on the most severe.
Exam cue: prioritize by risk, but never leave known high-risk findings with no owner or date.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-84 (Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IR-3 (Incident Response Testing)
questions.question: A firm has never tested its incident response plan. Which test should the CISO schedule FIRST?

options.A: A tabletop walk-through of a realistic scenario with key staff
options.B: A functional drill running the technical playbooks on live tools
options.C: An unannounced simulated attack against production systems
options.D: A review of another firm's published exercise results

questions.key_concept: Test incident response plans in stages: a tabletop first, then functional drills, then full-scale exercises.
questions.pre_read: Note the word never. Ask which test is safe and still checks the plan itself.
questions.correct_explanation: Testing should build in stages. A tabletop walk-through checks roles, decisions and plan logic at low risk, exposing basic gaps before anything touches live systems. Functional drills and full-scale exercises follow once the plan is sound. Running technical playbooks is valuable later, but on an untested plan it risks disruption and confusion over who decides what.

wrong_explanations.B: Functional drills are a later stage. On a plan never tested, they risk disruption before roles and decisions are even checked.
wrong_explanations.C: An unannounced attack on production is the riskiest test and is inappropriate before basic plan logic has been checked.
wrong_explanations.D: Another firm's results say nothing about whether this firm's plan, people and roles work.

tips: Eliminate: C starts with the riskiest live test, and D tests someone else's plan rather than this one.
Final two: A beats B because testing builds up from discussion to live action, starting with the lowest-risk check of the plan.
Exam cue: for a first test, pick the lowest-risk method that checks the plan itself, then build up.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-86 (Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response); ISO/IEC 27037 (Guidelines for Identification, Collection, Acquisition and Preservation of Digital Evidence); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.28 (Collection of Evidence)
questions.question: Malware is found on a file server that may be needed as evidence in legal action. What should the incident response team do FIRST?

options.A: Record the chain of custody after the analysis ends
options.B: Create a hashed forensic image before any analysis
options.C: Run antivirus scans on the live server to identify the malware
options.D: Delete the infected files to protect other users

questions.key_concept: Preserve before you analyse: take a hashed forensic image and keep chain of custody so evidence stays admissible.
questions.pre_read: Notice the words legal action. Ask which option keeps the evidence provably unchanged.
questions.correct_explanation: Evidence for legal action must be shown to be unaltered. Capturing a forensic image and recording its hash before analysis preserves the original state and lets later findings be verified against it. Scanning the live server seems a quick way to learn what happened, but it changes files and timestamps and may destroy the integrity that makes the evidence admissible.

wrong_explanations.A: Chain of custody must be recorded from the moment evidence is collected. Recording it afterwards leaves gaps a court may reject.
wrong_explanations.C: Scanning the live system alters files and timestamps, which can undermine the evidence's integrity before it is preserved.
wrong_explanations.D: Deleting files destroys evidence. Containment should isolate the server, not erase what investigators need.

tips: Eliminate: D destroys the evidence, and A leaves gaps in custody that a court may reject.
Final two: B beats C because preserving an unaltered, hashed copy must come before any analysis that could change the original.
Exam cue: when evidence may go to court, preserve first and analyse copies; never work on the original.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that during a ransomware attack, isolating infected servers waited four hours for the CEO's approval. Which recommendation BEST addresses this delay?

options.A: Pre-delegate containment authority to the incident manager
options.B: Require the whole response team to agree before isolating servers
options.C: Record each incident decision and its approver in a decision log
options.D: Route isolation decisions to the board risk committee instead

questions.key_concept: Containment is fast when the incident plan pre-delegates authority to act, so the incident manager need not wait for executive approval.
questions.pre_read: Notice that the delay came from waiting for one approver. Ask which change removes the wait rather than recording it.
questions.correct_explanation: The four-hour delay came from needing the CEO's approval before acting. Pre-delegating containment authority to the incident manager, within limits management sets in the plan, lets isolation happen in minutes while executives are briefed. A decision log is good practice for accountability and later review, but it records the delay rather than preventing it.

wrong_explanations.B: Requiring the whole team to agree adds another approval step and slows containment further. It spreads responsibility instead of assigning it.
wrong_explanations.C: A decision log supports accountability and post-incident review, but containment would still wait for the same executive approval.
wrong_explanations.D: Moving the decision to a board committee adds a higher, slower approval layer during a live attack.

tips: Eliminate: B adds a consensus step, and D moves the decision even higher; both slow containment further.
Final two: A beats C because pre-delegated authority removes the wait, while a decision log only records it.
Exam cue: when an incident stalls waiting for approval, look for authority delegated in advance through the plan.

questions.question: A server shows signs of fileless malware that runs only in memory, and an administrator wants to reboot it to restore service. What should the incident manager do FIRST?

options.A: Image the server's hard disk after a clean shutdown
options.B: Reboot the server and then run a full antivirus scan
options.C: Capture a memory image before the server is shut down
options.D: Restore the server from last night's backup image

questions.key_concept: Volatile evidence is lost on shutdown, so memory must be captured before a reboot when malware lives only in memory.
questions.pre_read: Notice the malware runs only in memory. Ask what evidence a reboot would destroy, and capture it before anything else.
questions.correct_explanation: Fileless malware leaves little or no trace on disk; its code, processes and network connections exist in memory and vanish on shutdown. Following the order of volatility, the incident manager should capture memory first, then image the disk. A disk image after a clean shutdown is sound forensic practice, but here it would miss the very evidence that shows what the malware did.

wrong_explanations.A: A disk image is valuable, but shutting down first destroys the memory where this fileless malware runs, losing the key evidence.
wrong_explanations.B: Rebooting wipes memory-resident evidence, and an antivirus scan is unlikely to find malware that never touched the disk.
wrong_explanations.D: Restoring from backup overwrites the system before evidence is collected and may restore the same weakness the attacker used.

tips: Eliminate: B reboots away the evidence, and D overwrites the system before anything is collected.
Final two: C beats A because fileless malware lives in memory; a disk image taken after shutdown misses it.
Exam cue: collect evidence in order of volatility, memory first, whenever a shutdown or reboot is about to happen.

questions.question: Malware is found on an engineering workstation that controls a chemical plant's reactor process. What should the incident manager do FIRST?

options.A: Disconnect the workstation from the plant network immediately
options.B: Confirm with plant operations that isolating it is safe
options.C: Reimage the workstation from the standard office desktop build
options.D: Leave the response to plant operations without security staff

questions.key_concept: In operational technology, human and process safety come first: check that isolation will not create a hazard before disconnecting control systems.
questions.pre_read: Notice the workstation controls a live chemical process. Ask what an abrupt disconnection could do to the plant before acting.
questions.correct_explanation: In operational technology the first priority is human and process safety. Abruptly disconnecting a workstation that controls a reactor could cause loss of view or control and create a hazard. The incident manager should confirm with plant operations how to isolate safely, then contain. Immediate disconnection is the standard IT reflex and is often right in office networks, but here it skips the safety check.

wrong_explanations.A: Instant disconnection is the IT reflex, but losing control of a live reactor process can create a safety hazard worse than the malware.
wrong_explanations.C: An office desktop build would remove the specialized control software, destroy evidence and could halt the process.
wrong_explanations.D: Plant staff know the process but not malware response. Excluding security staff leaves containment and evidence handling unmanaged.

tips: Eliminate: C wipes a specialized control system with an office build, and D removes security expertise from the response.
Final two: B beats A because safety comes first in plant control systems; disconnecting a reactor controller blindly may cause harm.
Exam cue: when an incident touches physical processes, check human safety before applying standard IT containment steps.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-86 (Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response); ISO/IEC 27037 (Guidelines for Identification, Collection, Acquisition and Preservation of Digital Evidence)
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews how the forensic team images laptops seized in investigations. Which finding should concern the auditor MOST?

options.A: Analysts examine working copies rather than the master image
options.B: Imaging is performed by one analyst without a second witness
options.C: Commercial imaging tools are used instead of open-source tools
options.D: Original drives are connected without a write-blocker

questions.key_concept: A write-blocker keeps the original drive unchanged during imaging; without it, the evidence itself may be altered in ways no later step can undo.
questions.pre_read: Ask which weakness changes the original evidence itself, and which only weakens the paperwork around it.
questions.correct_explanation: Connecting an original drive without a write-blocker lets the operating system write to it, changing timestamps and other data on the evidence itself. That alteration cannot be undone and gives opposing counsel a strong integrity challenge. A missing second witness weakens chain-of-custody records, but the image can still be verified against the original by hash values, so it is the lesser risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Working on copies protects the master image and is recommended practice, so this finding is not a weakness.
wrong_explanations.B: A witness strengthens custody records, but integrity can still be shown by comparing hash values of the original and the image.
wrong_explanations.C: Tool choice is not a control weakness. Validated commercial and open-source imaging tools are both acceptable.

tips: Eliminate: A describes good practice, and C is a tool preference rather than a control weakness.
Final two: D beats B because writing to the original alters evidence permanently, while a missing witness is a documentation gap.
Exam cue: in evidence handling, a flaw that changes the original outranks a flaw in the paperwork around it.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 (Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.23 (Information Security for Use of Cloud Services); ISO/IEC 27017 (Cloud Security)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds the company's cloud incident response plan assumes the cloud provider will investigate any breach of the company's hosted applications. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Apply the on-premises incident playbook unchanged to cloud incidents
options.B: Define the company's own investigation duties under shared responsibility
options.C: Obtain the provider's independent assurance report on incident handling
options.D: Remove the hosted applications from the plan's scope entirely

questions.key_concept: Under shared responsibility, the customer must investigate breaches of its own applications, data and identities; the provider covers only its layers.
questions.pre_read: Notice who the plan expects to investigate. Ask which layers the provider actually controls and which stay with the company.
questions.correct_explanation: Under the shared responsibility model, the provider secures and investigates its own infrastructure, but the customer remains responsible for its applications, data, identities and configurations. The plan must define the company's investigation duties, evidence sources and how it will request provider cooperation. The provider's assurance report shows the provider's controls are sound, but it cannot cover breaches in layers the company controls.

wrong_explanations.A: On-premises playbooks assume disk access and network taps the company does not have in the cloud, and ignore provider-specific evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: An assurance report covers the provider's own controls. It does not investigate breaches in applications the company configures and runs.
wrong_explanations.D: Removing hosted applications from scope leaves breaches of the company's own cloud workloads with no response at all.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores how cloud evidence differs, and D leaves cloud breaches with no response.
Final two: B beats C because the provider's report covers only its own layers; the company must investigate its own.
Exam cue: in cloud questions, the customer keeps responsibility for its data, identities and access under every service model.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-86 (Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.16 (Monitoring Activities)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that after a data theft, investigators had only network flow records and could not tell what data left. Which recommendation BEST improves future network forensics?

options.A: Retain the existing flow records for a longer period
options.B: Review firewall rule changes on a weekly schedule
options.C: Capture sampled packets during peak business hours
options.D: Capture full packets at the main internet exit points

questions.key_concept: Flow records show who talked to whom and how much, but only full packet capture shows the content that left.
questions.pre_read: Notice the gap is the content of the stolen data. Ask which evidence source records content rather than connection summaries.
questions.correct_explanation: Flow records summarize connections, showing addresses, ports, times and byte counts, but not what was sent. To establish what data left, investigators need full packet capture at strategic points such as the main internet exits, where all outbound traffic passes. Sampled capture during peak hours records some content, but attackers often move data off-hours, so the decisive packets would likely be missed.

wrong_explanations.A: Keeping flow records longer adds history but still records no content, so the same question would remain unanswered.
wrong_explanations.B: Reviewing firewall changes is a sound configuration control, but it produces no evidence of what data crossed the network.
wrong_explanations.C: Sampling misses most traffic, and exfiltration often happens outside peak hours, so the decisive packets may never be captured.

tips: Eliminate: A adds more of the same content-free data, and B is a configuration control, not evidence collection.
Final two: D beats C because sampling at peak hours misses most traffic, including off-hours exfiltration.
Exam cue: when the question is what data left, pick the source that records content, not summaries.
