questions.subtopic: SaaS Customer Material Data Breach, Notification, and Full Incident Response
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 33 (Notification of Personal Data Breach to Supervisory Authority); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.22 (Monitoring, Review and Change Management of Supplier Services); COBIT 2019 APO10 (Managed Vendors)
questions.question: A bank learns from news reports that its payroll SaaS provider suffered a breach, but the provider has sent no notice. What should the bank's CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Terminate the provider's contract for failing to give notice
options.B: Ask the provider whether the bank's data was exposed
options.C: Wait for the provider's formal notice before taking action
options.D: Tell employees that their payroll data was breached

questions.key_concept: An organization stays accountable for data its providers hold and must act promptly to learn whether that data was affected.
questions.pre_read: Notice the provider has not given notice. Ask who is accountable for the payroll data.
questions.correct_explanation: The bank remains accountable for its employees' payroll data even though a provider holds it, and its own notice duties may start once it becomes aware of a likely breach. Asking the provider at once whether bank data was exposed gives the facts needed to act. Waiting for formal notice seems orderly, but the provider is already silent, and the bank's own deadlines may be running.

wrong_explanations.A: Terminating mid-incident cuts off the information the bank needs and does not protect the exposed data.
wrong_explanations.C: The provider has already stayed silent. Waiting passively may let the bank's own notification deadlines pass.
wrong_explanations.D: Exposure is not yet confirmed. Telling employees their data was breached before checking is premature and may be wrong.

tips: Eliminate: A cuts off the source of facts, and D announces a breach that is not yet confirmed.
Final two: B beats C because the data owner stays accountable and must seek the facts; waiting leaves its own clock running.
Exam cue: outsourcing a service never outsources accountability for the data; the owner must act on its own.

questions.subtopic: Zero-Day Vulnerability Mitigation and Full Incident Response
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 RA-10 (Threat Hunting); NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 (Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management); NIST SP 800-40 Rev 4 (Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning)
questions.question: A flaw in a firm's VPN appliances was exploited worldwide for nine days before the vendor's patch, which the firm has now applied to every appliance. What should the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Hunt for compromise that occurred before the patch
options.B: Monitor the appliances closely for any new exploit attempts
options.C: Close the incident because every appliance is now patched
options.D: Replace the appliances with another vendor's product

questions.key_concept: Patching closes a vulnerability but does not evict attackers; hunt for compromise during the window it was exploited.
questions.pre_read: Notice the flaw was exploited for nine days before the patch. Ask what the patch cannot undo.
questions.correct_explanation: Nine days of worldwide exploitation means attackers may already have entered and planted backdoors or stolen credentials, and a patch closes the hole without removing them. Hunting for indicators of compromise from the exposure window shows whether the firm was breached. Watching for new exploit attempts sounds vigilant, but the patch already blocks those; the open question is what happened before it.

wrong_explanations.B: The patch now blocks new attempts. Watching for them ignores intrusions that may have happened during the nine days.
wrong_explanations.C: Patching closes the flaw but does not remove an attacker who entered before it was applied.
wrong_explanations.D: Changing vendors is a long-term decision that does nothing about a compromise that may already exist.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes patching removes intruders, and D is a long-term choice that ignores possible compromise.
Final two: A beats B because the patch already blocks new attempts; the risk now is an intrusion from before it.
Exam cue: after a flaw was exploited in the wild, patching is not the end; check for compromise during the exposure window.

questions.subtopic: Ransomware Detection in EDR. Primary Consideration
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 (Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management); #StopRansomware Guide (CISA, FBI, NSA, MS-ISAC, 2023); MITRE ATT&CK Framework Impact tactic (T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact)
questions.question: Ransomware is actively encrypting a shared file server, and about 7% of files are already locked. What should the CISO treat as the PRIMARY consideration when choosing the immediate response?

options.A: Meeting regulatory deadlines for reporting the service outage
options.B: Capturing memory from the server before anything is changed
options.C: Keeping the file server available to the engineering staff
options.D: Stopping the encryption and its spread without delay

questions.key_concept: While destruction is under way, halting it outweighs evidence capture; every minute adds more unrecoverable data and wider spread.
questions.pre_read: Notice the encryption is still running. Ask which consideration loses more value with every minute of delay.
questions.correct_explanation: Each minute of active encryption locks more files and gives the malware more chance to spread to other systems, so halting it dominates the immediate decision. Capturing memory is valuable for investigation, and good responders try to do it quickly, but it must not delay isolation while data is being destroyed. Evidence can still be collected from the isolated server.

wrong_explanations.A: Regulatory reporting matters, but its deadlines run in hours or days. It does not drive the next few minutes.
wrong_explanations.B: Memory capture helps investigators, but delaying isolation to collect it lets the malware lock more files and spread further.
wrong_explanations.C: An infected server cannot be kept usable safely. Keeping it online lets the encryption continue.

tips: Eliminate: A works on a slower clock than active encryption, and C keeps an infected server running.
Final two: D beats B because active destruction outweighs evidence capture; isolate first, collect evidence from the isolated server.
Exam cue: while damage is still happening, containment speed wins. Investigation needs come second.

questions.question: After a payment API key was found hard-coded in a published mobile app and was rotated, an IS auditor reviews the root cause. Which recommendation BEST prevents recurrence?

options.A: Rotate the payment API key every ninety days
options.B: Remove the developer's permission to publish app builds
options.C: Move the key to a back-end service the app calls
options.D: Retrain developers on safe handling of credentials in app code

questions.key_concept: Remove secrets from source code entirely; a technical control that removes the hazard beats relying on people to handle it safely.
questions.pre_read: Notice the root cause is a key inside code. Ask which option removes keys from code rather than asking people to be careful.
questions.correct_explanation: The root cause is that a live credential sat in the app's code, where anyone who unpacks the app can read it. Moving the key to a back-end service that the app calls at run time, with the secret held in a vault, takes it out of the app altogether, so a careless build exposes nothing. Retraining developers is worthwhile, but it still relies on every person getting it right every time.

wrong_explanations.A: Periodic rotation shortens the life of a leaked key but still leaves it exposed for weeks and does not stop the next leak.
wrong_explanations.B: Restricting one developer ignores the process gap. Any other developer could hard-code a key the same way.
wrong_explanations.D: Training helps, but it depends on people never making the same mistake, so the hazard remains in the code.

tips: Eliminate: A only shortens how long a leaked key works, and B blames one person for a process gap.
Final two: C beats D because taking the key out of the app removes the hazard; training still relies on flawless people.
Exam cue: when a human slip caused the incident, prefer the control that removes the chance to slip.

questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.12 (Data Leakage Prevention); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement); CERT Common Sense Guide to Mitigating Insider Threats, 7th Edition (CMU SEI, 2022)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds a data loss prevention tool alerted only after a departing research scientist emailed 1,800 confidential formula files to personal webmail. Which control would BEST have prevented the loss?

options.A: Exit interviews reminding leavers of their confidentiality duties
options.B: Blocking confidential attachments sent to personal email domains
options.C: Real-time review of data loss prevention alerts by analysts
options.D: Annual recertification of user access to formula files

questions.key_concept: Data loss prevention should block, not just alert on, transfers of classified data to unapproved destinations where the business case allows.
questions.pre_read: Notice the tool alerted only after the files were sent. Ask which option stops the files leaving rather than spotting it sooner.
questions.correct_explanation: The tool detected the transfer but did not stop it. Configuring it to block confidential attachments sent to personal email domains prevents the files from leaving at all, which matches the classification of the formula data. Faster review of alerts by security analysts is a real improvement, but it is still detective: files leave while someone reads the alert and reacts.

wrong_explanations.A: A reminder does not stop a determined employee, and exit interviews happen after resignation, often after the copying.
wrong_explanations.C: Faster alert review shortens the response, but it is detective. Emails already sent cannot be pulled back.
wrong_explanations.D: The scientist legitimately needed access to the formula files, so an annual recertification would have confirmed that access.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a reminder that comes too late, and D would have confirmed the scientist's legitimate access.
Final two: B beats C because blocking prevents the loss, while faster alert review still detects it afterward.
Exam cue: preventive controls come first where feasible; detection is the defense-in-depth layer behind them.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds one payables clerk both changed a supplier's bank details from an email and released a $380,000 payment to the fraudster. What should be the PRIMARY focus of the auditor's recommendation?

options.A: Separating supplier bank-detail changes from payment release duties
options.B: Training payables staff to recognize spoofed supplier emails
options.C: Adding a fraud loss endorsement to the cyber insurance policy
options.D: Disciplining the clerk who processed the fraudulent change

questions.key_concept: No single person should both change supplier bank details and release payments; segregation forces independent verification.
questions.pre_read: Notice one clerk did both steps. Ask which control means one deceived person cannot complete the fraud.
questions.correct_explanation: The loss happened because one person could both change where money goes and release it, so a single deceived clerk was enough. Separating bank-detail changes from payment release means a second person must verify each change, through a known contact, before money moves. Training staff to spot spoofed emails helps, but convincing fakes still get through, and nothing would stop one deceived person again.

wrong_explanations.B: Training helps, but convincing spoofs still succeed, and one deceived clerk could still change details and pay.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance may offset a loss, but it does not stop the next fraudulent payment from leaving.
wrong_explanations.D: Discipline targets one person and leaves the control gap that let one person do both steps.

tips: Eliminate: C transfers loss without preventing it, and D punishes a person while the control gap stays open.
Final two: A beats B because segregation stops one deceived person from completing the fraud; training relies on spotting every fake.
Exam cue: when one person could complete a fraud alone, the PRIMARY fix is segregation of duties.

questions.question: After a root key exposure, an IS auditor reviews the bank's hardware security module controls. Which finding should concern the auditor MOST?

options.A: The module firmware is one minor version behind the latest release
options.B: Issued certificates are valid for five years before renewal
options.C: Administrator activity logs are reviewed monthly, not daily
options.D: One administrator can export the root key without a second person

questions.key_concept: Root key operations need dual control and split knowledge so no single person or stolen credential can export the key.
questions.pre_read: Notice the key was exposed through one administrator credential. Ask which finding lets a single person do the damage again.
questions.correct_explanation: The root key is the most sensitive asset in the trust chain, so its export or use should require dual control, meaning at least two authorized people. A single administrator able to export it means one stolen credential is enough to repeat the compromise. Monthly log review is a real weakness, but it is detective: it would find a misuse weeks later, not prevent it.

wrong_explanations.A: A minor firmware lag deserves tracking, but it is not what allowed one credential to expose the key.
wrong_explanations.B: Long certificate lifetimes increase exposure if a certificate is compromised, but they do not protect the root key itself.
wrong_explanations.C: Slow log review delays detection, but daily review would still only find misuse after the key was taken.

tips: Eliminate: A is a minor patching gap, and B concerns certificate lifetimes, not protection of the root key.
Final two: D beats C because dual control prevents a single person exporting the key; faster log review only detects it.
Exam cue: for the most sensitive keys, look for dual control and split knowledge before monitoring improvements.

questions.question: A container in the build cluster escaped to its host node, which also runs the deployment job holding production cloud keys. What should the incident manager treat as the PRIMARY concern when scoping the incident?

options.A: Whether the image scanner should have caught the known flaw
options.B: How many unused image versions remain in the container registry
options.C: Whether workloads and credentials on that node are now compromised
options.D: Whether runtime alert rules were tuned to reduce false alarms

questions.key_concept: Scope follows the attacker's reach: an escape to the host exposes every workload and credential on that node.
questions.pre_read: Notice the escape reached the host. Ask what else the attacker can now touch, rather than how the flaw got in.
questions.correct_explanation: An escape gives the attacker the host node, and from there every workload on it, including the deployment job and its production cloud keys. Scoping must therefore start from what the attacker can now reach. Whether the image scanner missed the flaw is an important root-cause question, but it explains how the attacker got in, not how far the damage extends, and it belongs in the post-incident review.

wrong_explanations.A: The scanner gap is a root-cause finding for the lessons-learned review. It does not tell responders how far the attacker has reached.
wrong_explanations.B: Registry hygiene is a general housekeeping concern with no bearing on the scope of this live compromise.
wrong_explanations.D: Alert tuning matters for future detection, but the alert already fired. It does not define the incident's scope.

tips: Eliminate: B is registry housekeeping, and D concerns alert tuning after the alert already worked.
Final two: C beats A because scoping asks how far the attacker reached; how the flaw got in is a later root-cause question.
Exam cue: during scoping, follow the blast radius. Root-cause questions belong to the post-incident review.

questions.question: A disclosed web framework flaw has a severity score of 9.8 out of 10, working exploit code is circulating publicly, and affected applications face the internet. Which factor should MOST drive the security manager's urgency?

options.A: The vendor's contractual deadline for delivering a fix
options.B: Public exploit code against internet-facing applications
options.C: The flaw's critical severity score of 9.8
options.D: The number of users who might later need notification

questions.key_concept: Prioritize vulnerabilities by real exploitability and exposure, not by severity score alone.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem gives both a score and evidence of active exploit code. Ask which one shows that attack is likely now.
questions.correct_explanation: A severity score describes how bad exploitation would be, but working public exploit code against internet-facing systems shows that attack is likely right now, which is what sets urgency. That is why lists of known exploited vulnerabilities drive faster remediation than scores alone. The 9.8 score is a valid input, but many high-scoring flaws are never exploited, so the score by itself overstates or understates urgency.

wrong_explanations.A: The vendor's contract affects escalation, not the firm's exposure. Attackers do not wait for contractual deadlines.
wrong_explanations.C: A high score shows potential severity, but without exploit evidence and exposure it does not show attack is imminent.
wrong_explanations.D: Notification planning comes after exposure is assessed. It does not set how fast controls must be applied.

tips: Eliminate: A concerns the vendor's contract, and D is downstream notification planning.
Final two: B beats C because public exploit code against exposed systems shows likely attack; a score shows only potential severity.
Exam cue: in vulnerability questions, exploit availability and exposure outrank the raw severity score.

questions.question: A support agent typed credentials into a phishing page and approved the push prompt the attacker triggered. Which control should the security manager adopt to BEST prevent this account takeover?

options.A: Phishing-resistant authentication with FIDO2 security keys
options.B: Number matching on every push approval prompt
options.C: Text-message passcodes in place of push approvals
options.D: Longer, more complex password rules for support staff

questions.key_concept: Authenticators bound to the genuine site's origin, such as FIDO2 keys, cannot be relayed through a phishing page.
questions.pre_read: Notice the user was on a fake page that relayed the login. Ask which option still works for the attacker in that setup.
questions.correct_explanation: The attacker relayed the agent's login through a fake page, so any code or approval the user can see and enter can also be relayed. FIDO2 security keys bind the login to the genuine site's address, so a phishing page cannot use them. Number matching stops blind approval of random prompts, but a relaying phishing page can show the user the number to enter.

wrong_explanations.B: Number matching reduces push fatigue, but a real-time phishing proxy can display the matching number and the user will enter it.
wrong_explanations.C: Text-message codes are typed by the user and can be relayed through the phishing page just as easily.
wrong_explanations.D: The attacker captured the password directly. A longer password is phished just as easily.

tips: Eliminate: C swaps one relayable method for another, and D strengthens a password the attacker simply captures.
Final two: A beats B because origin-bound keys cannot be relayed; a phishing proxy can show the matching number.
Exam cue: when the attacker sits between the user and the real site, only phishing-resistant authentication stops the relay.

questions.question: An unapproved console change opened a database security group to the internet; the setting was restored from the infrastructure-as-code baseline. Before the CISO closes the incident, what should the IS auditor verify as MOST important?

options.A: The engineer who made the console change has been retrained
options.B: The baseline was reapplied successfully through the pipeline
options.C: The incident report was shared at the quarterly risk committee
options.D: Direct console changes to production security settings are now blocked

questions.key_concept: Closing an incident requires removing the path that caused it; restoring the baseline alone leaves the same bypass open.
questions.pre_read: Notice how the change was made. Ask whether the bypass still exists after the setting was restored.
questions.correct_explanation: The exposure happened because someone could change production security settings directly in the console, outside the approved pipeline. Until that bypass is blocked, the same drift can recur at any time. Confirming the baseline was reapplied proves the immediate fix worked, which matters, but it reverses the symptom rather than closing the cause, so the incident is not truly resolved.

wrong_explanations.A: Retraining one engineer leaves the console bypass open, so anyone else with console access could make the same unapproved change.
wrong_explanations.B: Successful reapplication confirms the immediate fix but leaves the console bypass that allowed the drift in place.
wrong_explanations.C: Reporting to the risk committee is good governance but does not remove the cause of the incident.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains one person while the bypass stays open, and C is reporting rather than remediation.
Final two: D beats B because blocking the bypass prevents recurrence; reapplying the baseline only reverses this occurrence.
Exam cue: before closing an incident, check that the root cause is removed, not just the symptom reversed.

questions.subtopic: SaaS Customer Material Data Breach. Notification First
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 33 (Notification of Personal Data Breach to Supervisory Authority); GDPR Article 34 (Data Subject Notification); GDPR Article 24 (Controller Responsibility)
questions.question: A SaaS firm has notified 47 business clients of a breach of their data; the breach also exposed the firm's own EU employee records. What should the firm's data protection officer verify is MOST important?

options.A: Every client has acknowledged receipt of the breach notice
options.B: The forensic report has been formatted for the audit committee
options.C: The firm's own regulator notice for employee data was filed
options.D: The incident is logged for the next quarterly risk report

questions.key_concept: Telling clients does not discharge an organization's own legal duties as controller of the data it owns.
questions.pre_read: Notice whose data the employee records are. Ask whose legal duty applies to them.
questions.correct_explanation: For the employee records, the firm itself is the data controller, so GDPR Article 33 requires it to notify its supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless the breach is unlikely to result in risk. Notifying clients covers their data, not the firm's own. Client acknowledgements are useful evidence that notices arrived, but they do not discharge the firm's separate legal duty for its employees' data.

wrong_explanations.A: Acknowledgements prove delivery of client notices but do nothing for the firm's own legal obligation for its employee data.
wrong_explanations.B: Formatting a report for the audit committee is governance housekeeping with no legal deadline attached.
wrong_explanations.D: Logging for a quarterly report is routine reporting. It does not meet any regulatory notification deadline.

tips: Eliminate: B is report formatting, and D is routine internal reporting with no legal deadline.
Final two: C beats A because the firm's own controller duty is a legal deadline that client notices do not satisfy.
Exam cue: in breach questions, ask whose data it is. The controller of that data owns the notification duty.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5; ISO/IEC 27001:2022
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a payroll clerk can change employees' bank account details without any review or approval. Which security objective does this weakness threaten MOST?

options.A: Integrity of the employees' payment details
options.B: Confidentiality of the employees' payment details
options.C: Availability of the payroll application to staff
options.D: Performance of the monthly payroll batch run

questions.key_concept: Integrity means data is changed only by authorized, controlled actions; unreviewed changes to payment details threaten it directly.
questions.pre_read: Notice the clerk is changing data, not reading or disclosing it. Match that action to the objective it affects.
questions.correct_explanation: The weakness lets one person alter bank details with no check, so payments could be redirected through unauthorized or erroneous changes. That is a threat to integrity, which protects data from improper modification. Confidentiality also sounds relevant because bank details are sensitive, but the clerk is authorized to see them; the gap is the unchecked ability to change them.

wrong_explanations.B: The clerk is authorized to view the data. The weakness is unreviewed changes, not disclosure to unauthorized people.
wrong_explanations.C: Nothing in the finding prevents staff from using the payroll application, so availability is not the affected objective.
wrong_explanations.D: Batch run speed is an operational performance matter, not a security objective.

tips: Eliminate: C concerns system uptime, and D is operational performance, not security.
Final two: A beats B because the clerk can change the data; viewing it is already authorized.
Exam cue: map the verb to the objective. Read or disclose means confidentiality, change means integrity, use means availability.

questions.subtopic: Access Control. AAA Authentication Authorization Accounting
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 (AC family, AU family, IA family)
questions.question: Four engineers share one administrator account, and each signs in with the account's multi-factor authentication token. Which access control objective should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Authentication of the account through its multi-factor token
options.B: Accountability for the actions taken through the account
options.C: Availability of the account during emergency changes
options.D: Encryption of data that the account transmits

questions.key_concept: Shared accounts break accountability: logs show the account, not the person, so actions cannot be traced to an individual.
questions.pre_read: Notice the token works, but four people use it. Ask what the logs can no longer tell you.
questions.correct_explanation: The token still authenticates the account, but four people share it, so logs record actions against the account rather than a person. Accountability, the accounting element of authentication, authorization and accounting, is lost: no action can be traced to an individual. Authentication looks like the gap, but the token is still checked at every sign-in; what sharing destroys is the link from each action to one person.

wrong_explanations.A: The token still confirms the account is being used. What fails is linking each action to one person.
wrong_explanations.C: Sharing an account tends to make it more available, not less. Availability is not the risk here.
wrong_explanations.D: Encryption protects data in transit. It has no bearing on who performed an administrative action.

tips: Eliminate: C is not reduced by sharing, and D concerns data in transit, not who acted.
Final two: B beats A because the token still works; what is lost is tracing each action to one person.
Exam cue: shared or generic accounts are an accountability finding. Look for the option about tracing actions to individuals.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management)
questions.question: A bank adds fingerprint login to its mobile app. Which biometric measure should the IS auditor review MOST when the concern is impostors gaining access?

options.A: The false rejection rate measured during testing
options.B: The time each fingerprint scan takes to complete
options.C: The number of fingers each user may enroll
options.D: The false acceptance rate measured during testing

questions.key_concept: The false acceptance rate measures how often biometrics accept impostors; false rejection measures inconvenience to genuine users.
questions.pre_read: Notice the concern is impostors. Ask which error type lets the wrong person in.
questions.correct_explanation: The false acceptance rate shows how often the system wrongly accepts someone who is not the enrolled user, which is exactly the impostor risk. The false rejection rate matters for usability, but it measures genuine users being turned away, and tuning to reduce it usually raises false acceptance.

wrong_explanations.A: False rejection affects genuine users' convenience, not impostor access.
wrong_explanations.B: Scan speed is a usability measure with no bearing on impostor access.
wrong_explanations.C: Enrolled finger count affects convenience, not how often impostors are accepted.

tips: Eliminate: B and C are usability details unrelated to impostor access.
Final two: D beats A because impostor risk is measured by false acceptance; false rejection is usability.
Exam cue: for security of biometrics, look at false acceptance; for user friction, false rejection.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-175B Rev 1; NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5
questions.question: A firm with 200 branch systems finds that managing a separate secret key for each pair of systems has become unworkable. Which approach should the security architect choose as BEST?

options.A: Share one secret key across the 200 branch systems
options.B: Email new pairwise secret keys to the branches each month
options.C: Give each system a key pair with certified public keys
options.D: Hash the data exchanged between the branch systems

questions.key_concept: Asymmetric cryptography scales key distribution: one key pair per system replaces a secret key for every pair.
questions.pre_read: Notice the problem is the number of keys. Ask which approach needs only one key pair per system.
questions.correct_explanation: Pairwise symmetric keys grow with the square of the number of systems, while asymmetric cryptography needs only one key pair per system, with public keys distributed through certificates. Monthly emailed keys at least rotate secrets, but they still require pairwise keys and send them over an insecure channel.

wrong_explanations.A: One shared key means compromising any branch exposes every exchange.
wrong_explanations.B: Emailing keys exposes them in transit and keeps the pairwise burden.
wrong_explanations.D: Hashing does not provide confidentiality for the exchanged data.

tips: Eliminate: A creates a single point of compromise, and D confuses hashing with encryption.
Final two: C beats B because key pairs remove the pairwise burden; emailed keys keep it and add exposure.
Exam cue: asymmetric cryptography solves key distribution at scale; symmetric keys alone scale poorly.

questions.subtopic: Access Control Models. RBAC ABAC DAC MAC
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-162 (ABAC); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 (AC family)
questions.question: A defense contractor must stop staff from sharing classified files with colleagues who lack clearance, even when the file's creator wants to share. Which access control model BEST fits?

options.A: Discretionary access control set by each file's owner
options.B: Mandatory access control using labels and clearances
options.C: Role-based access control assigned by job function
options.D: Network-based access control by office location

questions.key_concept: Mandatory access control enforces system-wide labels and clearances that individual users, even owners, cannot override.
questions.pre_read: Notice the creator's wishes must be overridden. Ask which model removes that choice from the user.
questions.correct_explanation: The requirement is that no user, not even the file's creator, can share classified data with someone lacking clearance. Mandatory access control enforces that: the system compares the file's classification label with the user's clearance, and users cannot override it. Role-based access control is widely used and grants access by job, but people in the same role may hold different clearances, and roles are not designed to enforce them.

wrong_explanations.A: Discretionary control lets the owner decide who gets access, which is exactly what the requirement forbids.
wrong_explanations.C: Roles group permissions by job, but they do not compare classification labels with individual clearances.
wrong_explanations.D: Location says nothing about a person's clearance. Uncleared staff can sit in the same office.

tips: Eliminate: A gives the owner the choice the stem forbids, and D uses location instead of clearance.
Final two: B beats C because only mandatory control enforces clearance against labels; roles group jobs, not clearances.
Exam cue: when even the owner must not decide, the answer is mandatory access control.

questions.subtopic: Zero Trust Architecture. NIST SP 800-207 Principles
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust Architecture)
questions.question: Under a zero trust program, a user's laptop fails a device-health check halfway through a session. Which policy response would the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: Re-evaluate access and restrict the session at once
options.B: Keep the session open until the user logs out
options.C: Log the failure for review at the end of the month
options.D: Disconnect every user on the same network segment

questions.key_concept: Zero trust re-evaluates access continuously, restricting sessions when identity, device or context changes.
questions.pre_read: Notice the health check failed mid-session. Ask whether earlier trust still holds.
questions.correct_explanation: Zero trust evaluates access continuously, so a change in device health triggers re-evaluation and the session is restricted or ended until the device is compliant. Logging the failure for review supports investigation, but it lets an unhealthy device keep accessing resources for weeks, which contradicts continuous verification.

wrong_explanations.B: Keeping the session open grants trust based on the earlier check, not current state.
wrong_explanations.C: Monthly review leaves an unhealthy device connected for weeks.
wrong_explanations.D: Disconnecting a whole segment punishes healthy devices and relies on network location.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts a stale check, and D acts on network location rather than the device.
Final two: A beats C because zero trust re-evaluates in real time; monthly review is far too late.
Exam cue: zero trust means continuous verification; a change in identity or device state changes access.
